lessons.title: Los planetas gigantes y sus lunas
lessons.summary: Júpiter, Saturno, Urano, Neptuno y sus mundos.

cards.title: Gigantes gaseosos y helados
cards.text: Júpiter y Saturno son sobre todo hidrógeno y helio. Urano y Neptuno tienen más «hielos» de agua, amoníaco y metano, por eso se les llama gigantes helados.

deep.x: The giant planets formed beyond the "frost line", where ice was abundant. Jupiter and Saturn grew cores big enough fast enough to capture vast hydrogen envelopes. Uranus and Neptune formed later or farther out, where material was sparser, so they captured less gas.

items: Dense core of rock and ice

deep.x: Inside the two kinds
Colours
Jupiter's bands come from ammonia clouds and unknown colouring compounds. Uranus and Neptune look blue-green because methane in their air absorbs red light.
Diamond rain?

Inside Uranus and Neptune, extreme pressure may break methane apart and squeeze the carbon into diamonds that sink slowly towards the core. Lab experiments with lasers have produced tiny diamonds under similar conditions.
Many known exoplanets are "mini-Neptunes", so understanding our own ice giants helps explain worlds across the galaxy.

cards.title: ¿Júpiter nos protege?
cards.text: La enorme gravedad de Júpiter desvía o captura muchos cometas y asteroides. Puede que proteja a los planetas interiores, aunque también puede enviarnos alguno.

deep.x: The popular idea is that Jupiter acts as a cosmic shield, catching or flinging away comets that would otherwise hit Earth. Reality is more mixed: simulations show Jupiter also nudges asteroids and comets into the inner Solar System.
Impacts on Jupiter

In 1994 comet Shoemaker–Levy 9, torn into 21 pieces by Jupiter's gravity, crashed into the planet over six days. The impacts left dark scars larger than Earth, watched by telescopes worldwide. Amateur astronomers still catch small flashes of impacts.
Shaping the Solar System

x: Jupiter's gravity stopped a planet forming in the asteroid belt
It may have migrated inwards and back out early on (the "Grand Tack"), keeping Mars small
Its resonances create gaps in the asteroid belt (Kirkwood gaps)

deep.x: Jupiter is less a bodyguard than a traffic controller: it shapes where small bodies go, for better and worse.

cards.title: Ío, la luna volcánica
cards.text: Ío, luna de Júpiter, es el lugar más volcánico que se conoce, con cientos de volcanes. La gravedad de Júpiter la estruja como una pelota antiestrés y calienta su interior.

deep.x: Io, slightly bigger than our Moon, is the most volcanically active body known, with over 400 active volcanoes. Some fountain sulphur plumes up to 400 km high; lava lakes are hotter than Earth's lavas.
Tidal heating

Io's orbit is slightly oval because Europa and Ganymede tug on it rhythmically. As Io moves closer and farther from Jupiter, its rocky body flexes by up to about 100 m, generating heat by friction like bending a paperclip back and forth.
The resonance
A colourful world
Sulphur compounds paint Io yellow, orange, red and white, giving it the look of a pizza. It has almost no impact craters, because lava resurfaces it constantly.
Linda Morabito discovered Io's volcanoes in 1979 while processing Voyager images for navigation: she noticed a strange bump on the moon's edge.

cards.title: El océano de Europa
cards.text: Bajo la corteza helada de Europa hay un océano salado con quizá el doble de agua que todos los océanos de la Tierra. La Europa Clipper de la NASA, lanzada en 2024, lo estudiará.

deep.x: Europa, slightly smaller than our Moon, has a smooth icy crust criss-crossed by cracks and ridges. Beneath an ice shell perhaps 15–25 km thick lies a global salty ocean around 60–150 km deep, kept liquid by tidal heating.
Evidence for an ocean

x: Galileo detected a magnetic signal consistent with a salty, conductive ocean
Few craters: the surface is young and constantly renewed
"Chaos terrain" looks like icebergs that broke, shifted and refroze
Hubble and Webb spotted possible water plumes and surface CO₂

deep.x: Why it's exciting
The ocean is in contact with rock, which could supply chemical energy like Earth's deep-sea vents. Water, energy and chemistry are the three ingredients for life.
Europa Clipper

Launched in October 2024, Europa Clipper will make about 50 flybys from 2030, measuring the ice thickness, ocean saltiness and surface chemistry. It's the largest planetary spacecraft NASA has built, with solar panels over 30 m across.
Europa probably holds about twice as much liquid water as all of Earth's oceans combined.

cards.title: Ganímedes
cards.text: Ganímedes, otra luna de Júpiter, es la luna más grande del sistema solar, mayor que el planeta Mercurio, y tiene su propio campo magnético.

deep.x: Ganymede is 5,268 km wide, bigger than Mercury, though only half its mass because it's made largely of ice. It's the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field, which creates small auroras around it.
A layered world
Ganymede likely has an iron core, a rocky mantle, and thick ice layers sandwiching a salty ocean that may hold more water than Earth's oceans.
Two kinds of terrain

x: Dark, ancient regions heavily cratered
Lighter, grooved terrain where the ice was cracked and resurfaced

deep.x: ESA's JUICE
The JUpiter ICy moons Explorer, launched in 2023, will arrive in 2031 and later become the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than ours: Ganymede.
Galileo discovered Ganymede in 1610; it was named after a Trojan prince carried off by Zeus.

cards.title: Titán
cards.text: Titán, luna de Saturno, tiene una densa atmósfera anaranjada y lagos de metano y etano líquidos. La sonda Huygens aterrizó allí en 2005.

deep.x: Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, about 1.5 times Earth's surface pressure, mostly nitrogen. At −179 °C, methane plays the role water plays on Earth: it forms clouds, rain, rivers, lakes and seas.
Huygens' landing
In January 2005 ESA's Huygens probe parachuted through the orange haze for 2.5 hours and landed on a damp plain strewn with rounded "pebbles" of water ice: the most distant landing ever made.
Lakes and seas
Kraken Mare, the largest sea, is bigger than the Caspian Sea. Waves are rare and the liquid is clear enough that Cassini's radar saw to the bottom in places.
Dragonfly
NASA's Dragonfly, a car-sized nuclear-powered drone, is planned to launch in 2028 and fly between sites on Titan in the 2030s, studying prebiotic chemistry.
With low gravity and thick air, a human on Titan could fly by flapping strapped-on wings.

cards.title: Saturno flota
cards.text: La densidad media de Saturno es menor que la del agua. En una bañera lo bastante grande flotaría, aunque es una bola de gas, no un sólido.

deep.x: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm³, less than water's 1 g/cm³. It's mostly hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements. Of course, no bathtub is big enough, and Saturn would dissolve rather than bob, but the comparison shows how light it is.
Flattened by spin
Saturn spins once every 10.7 hours. Combined with its low density, that makes it the most flattened planet: its equator is about 10% wider than its pole-to-pole diameter.
The hexagon
At Saturn's north pole, a jet stream forms a six-sided pattern, each side wider than Earth. It's a stable wave pattern in the atmosphere and has lasted at least since Voyager saw it in 1981.
Many moons
Saturn has the most known moons of any planet, over 270, mostly small irregular ones captured long ago.

x: Titan: thick atmosphere
Enceladus: water plumes
Mimas: a giant crater that makes it look like the Death Star
Iapetus: one side dark, one side bright

deep.x: Saturn radiates more heat than it receives from the Sun, partly because helium "rain" sinks inside it and releases energy.

cards.title: Urano, de lado
cards.text: Urano está inclinado unos 98°, así que rueda alrededor del Sol de lado. Cada polo tiene 42 años de luz continua y luego 42 años de noche.

deep.x: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so its axis lies almost in the plane of its orbit. It likely suffered one or more huge collisions early in its history that knocked it over.
Extreme seasons
During one part of its orbit, a pole points almost straight at the Sun; half an orbit later, it points away. Each pole gets about 42 years of daylight followed by 42 years of darkness.

events.l: Voyager 2 sees the south pole facing the Sun

deep.x: Discovery

William Herschel found Uranus in 1781 with a homemade telescope, the first planet discovered since antiquity. He wanted to name it after King George III ("Georgium Sidus"); astronomers chose Uranus, father of Saturn.
Mysteries

x: Uranus barely emits more heat than it receives, unlike the other giants
Its magnetic field is tilted 59° and offset from the centre
It has 13 faint rings and 28 known moons named after Shakespeare and Pope characters

deep.x: Scientists have ranked a dedicated Uranus orbiter as a top priority for the coming decades.

cards.title: Los vientos de Neptuno

steps: Urano se desvía en su órbita

cards.text: Neptuno, el planeta más lejano, tiene los vientos más rápidos del sistema solar, de más de 2000 km/h. Se descubrió en 1846 gracias a las matemáticas, antes de que nadie lo viera.

deep.x: Neptune has the fastest winds measured in the Solar System, up to about 2,100 km/h, despite receiving only 1/900th of the sunlight Earth does. The energy likely comes from heat escaping its interior.
Discovered with maths

Astronomers noticed Uranus drifting from its predicted path. Urbain Le Verrier calculated where an unseen planet must be pulling it. On 23 September 1846, Johann Galle pointed a telescope there and found Neptune within 1° of the prediction.
Triton

Neptune's largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards, a sign it was captured, probably from the Kuiper Belt. Voyager 2 saw geysers of nitrogen erupting from its frozen surface. Tides are slowly dragging it inwards.

x: Neptune completed its first full orbit since discovery only in 2011
The Great Dark Spot seen in 1989 later vanished, and new spots have appeared

deep.x: Galileo actually saw Neptune in 1612 and 1613, but thought it was a star.

cards.title: Visitas a los gigantes
cards.text: Solo la Voyager 2 ha visitado Urano y Neptuno, en 1986 y 1989. Galileo y Juno estudiaron Júpiter; Cassini orbitó Saturno durante 13 años.

deep.x: Every close look at the outer planets has come from a handful of robotic spacecraft. Their flybys and orbits transformed points of light into worlds.
Cassini's grand finale

After 13 years at Saturn, nearly out of fuel, Cassini dived between the planet and its rings 22 times, then plunged into Saturn's atmosphere in September 2017. Burning it up ensured it could never contaminate Enceladus or Titan.
What they found
Why so few?
Missions to the outer planets are long (years to decades) and need nuclear power, because sunlight is weak far from the Sun. Each one is a once-in-a-generation project.
Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune, almost 40 years ago.

cards.title: Las capas del Sol
cards.text: La energía se produce en el núcleo, avanza lentamente hacia fuera por la zona radiativa durante decenas de miles de años, sube burbujeando por la zona convectiva y escapa por la superficie.

deep.x: The Sun has no solid surface. Its structure is defined by how energy moves outward from the core.
The slow escape

In the radiative zone, a photon of light is absorbed and re-emitted countless times in random directions. This "random walk" means energy takes from about 10,000 to 170,000 years to cross it. Then, in the convective zone, hot plasma rises like boiling soup, carrying energy to the surface in weeks.

steps: Random walk through radiative zone, ~100,000 years

deep.x: Granulation
The photosphere looks grainy in close-up: granules around 1,000 km wide, about twice the length of Portugal, the tops of convection cells, each lasting about 8–20 minutes before being replaced.

x: Core: about a quarter of the Sun's radius, where almost all fusion happens
Density at the core is about 150 times that of water

deep.x: We can "see" inside the Sun with helioseismology: tracking sound waves that make its surface ripple, much as earthquakes reveal Earth's interior.

cards.title: Caliente y más caliente
cards.text: La superficie está a unos 5500 °C, pero la atmósfera exterior, la corona, supera el millón de grados. Por qué está tan caliente sigue investigándose.

deep.x: Moving away from a heater, it gets colder. But above the Sun's 5,500 °C surface, the temperature rises dramatically: the thin corona reaches 1–3 million °C. This "coronal heating problem" has puzzled scientists since the 1940s.
Leading explanations

x: **Nanoflares**: countless tiny magnetic explosions continuously heating the corona
**Waves**: magnetic waves carrying energy up from below and dissipating
Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter are testing both by flying close

deep.x: Hot but not dense
The corona is extremely thin, so even at millions of degrees it holds little heat energy. You'd freeze before you'd cook, if the Sun's light didn't get you first.
Seeing the corona
The corona is normally hidden by the bright surface. It appears during a total solar eclipse as pearly streamers, or with coronagraphs, telescopes that block the Sun's disc.
Temperature measures how fast particles move, not how much heat they carry; the corona's particles are fast but few.

cards.title: Manchas solares
cards.text: Las manchas solares son zonas más frías y oscuras donde los campos magnéticos bloquean el calor. Su número sube y baja a lo largo de un ciclo solar de 11 años.

deep.x: Sunspots appear where intense magnetic fields poke through the surface and block the upward flow of heat. They're about 1,500 °C cooler than their surroundings, so they look dark, although on their own they'd glow brightly.
The 11-year cycle
Sunspot numbers rise and fall roughly every 11 years. At each solar maximum, the Sun's magnetic poles flip. Solar Cycle 25 peaked around 2024–25, producing strong auroras.
Size
Big sunspots can be several times wider than Earth. Groups often come in pairs with opposite magnetic polarity, like the ends of a bar magnet poking out.
The Maunder Minimum
From about 1645 to 1715, sunspots almost vanished. This coincided with part of the "Little Ice Age", though volcanic eruptions and other factors also played a role.
Galileo used sunspots to show that the Sun rotates and is not a perfect, unchanging sphere.
Never look at sunspots directly; use projection or a certified solar filter.

cards.title: Fulguraciones solares
cards.text: Las fulguraciones son estallidos repentinos de energía provocados por campos magnéticos enredados. Las grandes pueden alterar la radio, el GPS y los satélites en la Tierra.

deep.x: A flare happens when twisted magnetic field lines above sunspots suddenly snap and reconnect, releasing energy equal to millions of hydrogen bombs in minutes. Flares emit X-rays and ultraviolet light that reach Earth in about 8 minutes.
Flare classes
Coronal mass ejections

Flares often come with coronal mass ejections (CMEs): billions of tonnes of plasma hurled into space at hundreds to thousands of km/s. A CME takes 1–3 days to reach Earth, and it's the CME, not the flare, that drives big geomagnetic storms.
Effects on Earth

x: Radio blackouts for aircraft and ships
GPS errors and satellite damage
Extra drag that can bring satellites down early: in 2022, about 38 new satellites were lost after a storm
Higher radiation on polar flights

deep.x: The strongest flare ever recorded, in November 2003, saturated the sensors measuring it; it was later estimated at around X28 to X45.

cards.title: Viento solar
cards.text: El Sol lanza continuamente partículas cargadas al espacio a unos 400 km/s. El campo magnético de la Tierra desvía la mayoría.

deep.x: The corona is so hot that the Sun's gravity can't hold it: it streams away as the solar wind, a constant flow of electrons and protons. The slow wind travels at about 400 km/s; the fast wind, from coronal holes, at about 750 km/s.
The heliosphere
The solar wind inflates a vast bubble, the heliosphere, that protects the Solar System from much galactic radiation. Voyager 1 crossed its edge, the heliopause, in 2012 at about 121 AU.
Earth's shield
Earth's magnetic field deflects most of the solar wind, forming the magnetosphere, which is squashed on the Sun side and stretched into a long tail on the night side.

steps: Some particles funnel to the poles

x: The Sun loses about 1.5 million tonnes per second to the solar wind
Comet ion tails point straight away from the Sun because the wind pushes them

deep.x: Mars, without a global magnetic field, had much of its atmosphere stripped by the solar wind.

cards.title: Auroras
cards.text: Cuando las partículas solares chocan con la alta atmósfera cerca de los polos, el oxígeno brilla en verde y rojo, y el nitrógeno en azul y morado: son las auroras boreales y australes.

deep.x: Charged particles from the solar wind and CMEs are funnelled along Earth's magnetic field lines towards the poles. At 100–300 km altitude they collide with oxygen and nitrogen, exciting them to glow, like a neon sign.
Colours and heights
The auroral ovals

Auroras normally form in rings around the magnetic poles: northern Norway, Iceland, Canada and Alaska. During strong storms the ovals expand towards the equator. In May 2024 and October 2024, auroras were photographed from Portugal.

v.unit: Kp index needed to see auroras (approx.)

deep.x: Tips

x: Phone cameras often capture colour the eye can't see in faint auroras
Watch the Kp index and space weather forecasts
Look north, away from city lights

deep.x: Jupiter and Saturn have permanent auroras far more powerful than Earth's, powered partly by their own moons.

cards.title: El evento Carrington
cards.text: En 1859, una enorme tormenta solar hizo visibles las auroras cerca de los trópicos y dio descargas eléctricas a los telegrafistas. Hoy, una tormenta parecida podría dañar las redes eléctricas.

deep.x: On 1 September 1859, British astronomer Richard Carrington saw a brilliant white flare on the Sun. Seventeen hours later, a massive CME hit Earth. Auroras lit up skies as far south as Cuba and Hawaii; people in the Rocky Mountains woke thinking it was dawn.
Telegraph chaos
Telegraph lines sparked and some operators got shocks. Remarkably, some operators disconnected their batteries and sent messages using only the current induced by the storm.
If it happened today

A storm of that size could induce currents that damage high-voltage transformers, causing long blackouts, and could disable many satellites and disrupt GPS. Studies estimate global costs in the trillions.
Near misses

x: 1989: a smaller storm blacked out Quebec for 9 hours
2012: a Carrington-class CME missed Earth by about nine days of orbit

deep.x: Grid operators now have procedures to protect transformers when big storms are forecast.

cards.title: Previsión del tiempo espacial
cards.text: Varias naves vigilan el Sol para avisar de tormentas con un día o más de antelación, y así los operadores de satélites y de redes eléctricas pueden prepararse.

deep.x: Space weather forecasters watch the Sun constantly, much like meteorologists watch the atmosphere. Spacecraft such as SOHO and the Solar Dynamics Observatory image eruptions, and probes at the L1 point, 1.5 million km sunward, measure the solar wind before it hits Earth.
Scales
Who uses it

x: Power grid operators reduce load on vulnerable transformers
Airlines reroute polar flights to avoid radiation and radio blackouts
Satellite operators safe-mode their spacecraft
Astronauts shelter in shielded parts of the station

deep.x: Forecast limits
It's easy to see a CME leave, but hard to predict how strong its effect will be: that depends on the direction of its magnetic field, only measured when it reaches L1, under an hour before arrival.
Space weather is now listed among national risks in many countries, alongside pandemics and floods.

cards.title: Nunca lo mires directamente

items.r: Usa solo gafas de eclipse homologadas

cards.text: Mirar al Sol, aunque sea un momento durante un eclipse parcial, puede dañar tu retina para siempre. Usa gafas de eclipse homologadas o proyecta la imagen.

deep.x: The eye's lens focuses sunlight onto the retina like a magnifying glass. Staring at the Sun can burn retinal cells (solar retinopathy) without any pain, because the retina has no pain receptors. Damage can be permanent.
Partial eclipses are the danger
On a normal day, the Sun's glare makes you look away. During a partial eclipse, the sky darkens and people stare longer, but the visible sliver is just as intense.

deep.w: Sunglasses are enough
deep.r: Even dark sunglasses let through far too much light

deep.x: Safe ways

x: Certified eclipse glasses meeting ISO 12312-2
Pinhole projector: a hole in card projecting the Sun onto paper
Telescopes only with proper solar filters on the front
Welding glass of shade 12–14

deep.x: Totality exception
During the brief total phase of a total eclipse, it's safe to look without glasses, but put them back on the moment the Sun reappears.
A colander or the gaps between tree leaves make dozens of tiny crescent images on the ground during a partial eclipse.

cards.title: Parker Solar Probe
cards.text: Lanzada en 2018, la Parker Solar Probe de la NASA ha atravesado la corona y es el objeto fabricado por el ser humano más rápido, con unos 690 000 km/h.

deep.x: Parker Solar Probe, named after Eugene Parker who predicted the solar wind in 1958, is designed to "touch the Sun". On 24 December 2024 it passed just 6.1 million km from the surface, the closest any spacecraft has come.
Surviving the heat

A 11.4 cm thick carbon-composite heat shield faces the Sun at up to about 1,400 °C, while the instruments behind it stay near room temperature. The probe must keep the shield perfectly angled, doing so autonomously.
Getting close is hard

It's harder to reach the Sun than to leave the Solar System: Earth's orbital speed carries you sideways, and you must cancel it to fall in. Parker used seven Venus flybys to slow down and tighten its orbit.
What it's found

x: Magnetic "switchbacks": S-shaped kinks in the solar wind
A dust-free zone near the Sun
Direct measurements inside the corona for the first time

deep.x: Eugene Parker became the first person to see a spacecraft named after him launched, at age 91.

quiz.q: ¿Qué causa las manchas solares?
options: Campos magnéticos que bloquean el calor
quiz.explain: Son zonas más frías.

quiz.q: ¿Qué produce las auroras?
options: Partículas solares que chocan con la alta atmósfera
quiz.explain: El oxígeno brilla en verde y rojo.

lessons.title: El Big Bang
lessons.summary: Cómo empezó y creció el universo.

cards.title: Un universo en expansión
cards.text: En 1929, Edwin Hubble demostró que las galaxias lejanas se alejan de nosotros, y cuanto más lejos están, más rápido. Es el propio espacio el que se expande.

deep.x: In the 1910s Vesto Slipher measured the spectra of "spiral nebulae" and found most were redshifted: moving away from us. In 1929 Edwin Hubble combined these speeds with distances and found a simple pattern: the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes.
What it means
This isn't galaxies flying through space away from us in particular. Space itself is stretching, carrying galaxies apart. Every observer in every galaxy would see the same pattern.
Not everything expands
Galaxies, solar systems and atoms don't grow: gravity and other forces hold them together. Expansion only wins over huge distances between galaxy groups.
Einstein originally added a "cosmological constant" to keep the universe static; after Hubble's discovery he dropped it.

cards.title: Rebobinar
cards.text: Si todo se está separando, antes estuvo más junto. Rebobina la película unos 13 800 millones de años y todo estaba extremadamente caliente y denso: el Big Bang.

deep.x: If galaxies are moving apart now, they were closer in the past. Run the expansion backwards and everything converges into a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. That early hot phase, and the expansion from it, is what scientists call the Big Bang.

steps: 13.8 billion years ago: the Big Bang

deep.x: Measuring the age
What it doesn't say

The Big Bang theory describes how the universe evolved from a hot, dense state. It doesn't explain what, if anything, came "before" or what caused it; physics as we know it breaks down at the very beginning.

deep.w: The Big Bang explains the origin of everything
deep.r: It describes the evolution from a hot, dense early state; the very beginning is still unknown

deep.x: Three pillars of evidence

x: Galaxies receding in proportion to distance
The cosmic microwave background, leftover heat from the early universe
The amounts of hydrogen, helium and lithium, matching predictions

deep.x: No other theory explains all three pieces of evidence as well.

cards.title: No fue una explosión en el espacio

items.r: El espacio se estira en todas partes

cards.text: El Big Bang no fue una bomba que estalló en un espacio vacío. Fue la rápida expansión del propio espacio, en todas partes a la vez.

deep.x: The name suggests a bomb going off at a point, with debris flying into empty space. But the Big Bang happened everywhere at once: it was space itself expanding, not things flying through pre-existing space.
No centre
Because every point in space was part of the early dense universe, there's no special place where it "happened". Wherever you are, the Big Bang happened there too.
Faster than light?
Very distant galaxies recede faster than light. That doesn't break relativity: nothing is moving through space faster than light; space between us is stretching.

steps: Distant galaxies recede faster than light

deep.x: Inflation

Many cosmologists think a tiny fraction of a second after the start, space expanded extremely fast, by a factor of at least 10²⁶, in "cosmic inflation". It would explain why the universe is so smooth and flat.
The term "Big Bang" was coined by Fred Hoyle, who didn't believe in it, and the theory's main early proponent was a Catholic priest, Georges Lemaître.

cards.title: El pan de pasas
cards.text: Imagina pasas en una masa que sube: cada pasa ve que todas las demás se alejan, y las más lejanas se alejan más deprisa. No hay centro.

deep.x: Picture a loaf of raisin bread rising in the oven. Each raisin sees every other raisin moving away, and raisins twice as far apart separate twice as fast. No raisin is at the centre.
The balloon version

Another analogy: dots drawn on a balloon spread apart as it inflates. It shows there's no centre on the surface, but suggests a 3D centre inside the balloon, which doesn't exist for the real universe.
Doing the maths
If every distance doubles in an hour, a raisin 1 cm away ends up 2 cm away (moved 1 cm), while one 3 cm away ends up 6 cm away (moved 3 cm). Speed is proportional to distance: exactly Hubble's law.
All analogies break somewhere; the universe may have no edge and may be infinite.

cards.title: Los primeros minutos
cards.text: En los tres primeros minutos, el universo se enfrió lo suficiente para que protones y neutrones formaran núcleos de hidrógeno y helio. Los elementos más pesados llegaron mucho después, de las estrellas.

deep.x: In the first second, the universe was a hot soup of particles. As it expanded and cooled, quarks bound into protons and neutrons. Between about 1 and 3 minutes, protons and neutrons fused into nuclei: Big Bang nucleosynthesis.
The recipe

By the time fusion stopped, ordinary matter was about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with traces of deuterium and lithium. Measurements of the oldest gas clouds and stars match these predictions closely.
Why fusion stopped

The universe was cooling and thinning too fast. Unlike stars, which fuse for billions of years, the early universe had only minutes, so it couldn't build heavy elements. Those came much later, in stars.

steps: Too thin and cold to continue

deep.x: The amount of helium in the universe was a key test: the Big Bang predicted about 25%, and that's what we observe.

cards.title: El resplandor residual
cards.text: Unos 380 000 años después del Big Bang, el universo se volvió transparente. Esa luz todavía llena el espacio en forma de débiles microondas, descubiertas por casualidad en 1965.

deep.x: For 380,000 years the universe was a glowing fog of charged particles that scattered light. When it cooled to about 3,000 °C, electrons joined nuclei to form neutral atoms and light could travel freely. That light still fills the universe, stretched by expansion into microwaves at 2.7 K (−270 °C).
Found by accident

In 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, testing a radio antenna in New Jersey, found an annoying hiss coming from every direction. They even cleaned pigeon droppings from the antenna. The hiss was the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and they won the 1978 Nobel Prize.
The baby picture of the universe
The CMB is almost perfectly uniform, but has tiny temperature ripples, about 1 part in 100,000. These were the seeds of all later structure: galaxies and clusters grew from them.
About 1% of the static on an old analogue TV tuned between channels came from the cosmic microwave background.

cards.title: Corrimiento al rojo
cards.text: La luz de las galaxias que se alejan se estira hacia longitudes de onda más largas y rojas, como una sirena que suena más grave al alejarse.

deep.x: Light from receding objects has its wavelengths stretched towards the red end of the spectrum. For distant galaxies, the stretching is mostly due to space expanding while the light travels: cosmological redshift.
Measuring it

Astronomers find known spectral lines, like hydrogen's, and see how much they've shifted. The redshift "z" says how much the universe has expanded since the light left: z = 1 means wavelengths doubled.
Doppler on Earth
The same principle, for sound, makes an ambulance siren drop in pitch as it passes. Police radar guns use a Doppler shift to measure car speeds.
The record-holding galaxies seen by Webb have redshifts above 14: their light has been stretched more than 15 times.

cards.title: El universo observable
cards.text: Solo podemos ver hasta donde a la luz le ha dado tiempo a llegarnos. Como el espacio se expandió mientras tanto, el límite de lo que vemos está a unos 46 000 millones de años luz.

deep.x: We can only see objects whose light has had time to reach us since the universe became transparent. Because space kept expanding while the light travelled, the most distant objects we see are now about 46 billion light-years away, not 13.8.
Observable vs entire
The whole universe is likely much larger than the observable part, possibly infinite. What lies beyond our horizon is, in principle, unobservable.
A shrinking view

Because expansion is accelerating, distant galaxies are slipping beyond our reach. In the far future, observers in the Milky Way (merged with Andromeda) would see only their own merged galaxy, with the rest of the universe invisible.

deep.w: The universe is 13.8 billion light-years across
deep.r: The observable part is about 93 billion light-years across, thanks to expansion

deep.x: Being "13.8 billion years old" and "46 billion light-years in radius" aren't contradictory: space stretched while the light travelled.

cards.title: ¿Quién le puso nombre?
cards.text: Fred Hoyle, que prefería un universo «estacionario», acuñó «Big Bang» en la radio de la BBC en 1949. Georges Lemaître, sacerdote y físico belga, fue quien propuso la idea.

deep.x: In 1927 Georges Lemaître, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, proposed that the universe was expanding. In 1931 he suggested it began from a "primeval atom". The idea was controversial for decades.

events.l: Gamow and Alpher's hot Big Bang

deep.x: Steady state
Fred Hoyle, Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold proposed the steady-state theory: the universe expands, but new matter appears continuously so it always looks the same, with no beginning.
The name

On BBC radio in 1949, Hoyle called the rival theory "this big bang idea". He insisted he didn't mean it as an insult, but the catchy name stuck. The 1965 discovery of the CMB decisively favoured the Big Bang.
Science and faith
Pope Pius XII welcomed the Big Bang as support for creation; Lemaître himself asked him not to mix science and theology so directly, keeping the two separate.
Hoyle, though wrong about steady state, made major contributions, including explaining how stars make carbon.

cards.title: ¿Cómo acabará?
cards.text: La mayoría de las pruebas apuntan a un universo que se expandirá para siempre, cada vez más frío y oscuro durante un tiempo inimaginable: la «muerte térmica». Otros finales siguen debatiéndose.

deep.x: The universe's future depends on dark energy. If it stays constant, as current data mostly suggest, expansion accelerates forever.

items: Big Rip: dark energy tears everything apart
Big Bounce: crunch leads to a new bang

deep.x: The heat death timeline
Why "heat death"?
The universe would reach maximum entropy: everything at the same cold temperature, so no energy flows and nothing can happen. Not hot, but uniform.
New uncertainty
In 2024–25 the DESI galaxy survey reported hints that dark energy may be weakening. If so, the long-term future could change, possibly even towards a slowdown. More data is needed.
These timescales are so vast that the entire history of the universe so far is a tiny flicker at the very start.

quiz.q: ¿Qué edad tiene el universo?
quiz.explain: Se mide por la expansión y el resplandor residual.

quiz.q: ¿Qué descubrió Hubble en 1929?
options: Que las galaxias se alejan de nosotros
quiz.explain: El universo se expande.

lessons.title: Agujeros negros
lessons.summary: Los objetos más extraños del universo.

cards.title: El horizonte de sucesos
cards.text: El límite de un agujero negro es el horizonte de sucesos: el punto sin retorno. Dentro, la velocidad de escape supera la de la luz.

deep.x: The event horizon is a boundary in spacetime, not a physical surface. Outside it, a rocket with enough thrust can escape. Inside it, every possible path, even for light, leads inward.
Its size
The radius of the event horizon, the Schwarzschild radius, is proportional to mass: about 3 km per solar mass.
What you'd see

x: Approaching, the sky would distort as light bends around the black hole
Behind you, the universe's light would crowd into a shrinking circle
Crossing a large black hole's horizon, you'd notice nothing special at that moment

items.b: ~38 billion km wide, bigger than the Solar System's planets' orbits

deep.w: The event horizon is a solid surface
deep.r: It's an invisible boundary; nothing special happens to a falling observer at that point

deep.x: Once inside, the singularity is not a place in front of you but a moment in your future.

cards.title: Cómo se forman
cards.text: La mayoría de los agujeros negros estelares se forman cuando una estrella de más de unas 20 veces la masa del Sol agota su combustible y su núcleo colapsa.

deep.x: Stellar black holes form when the core of a massive star collapses. Above about 2–3 solar masses, no known force can stop a dead core collapsing: not even the pressure of tightly packed neutrons.
Other routes

items: Direct collapse of gas clouds, early universe
Primordial: maybe from the Big Bang

deep.x: Failed supernovae
Some massive stars may collapse straight into black holes without a bright explosion, simply vanishing. Astronomers have watched a few candidate stars disappear.
Growing
Black holes grow by swallowing gas, stars and other black holes. Mergers detected by gravitational waves often produce black holes of 30–150 solar masses.
The first confirmed black hole, Cygnus X-1, was identified in the 1970s from X-rays emitted by gas falling in from a companion star.

cards.title: Tamaño
cards.text: Si el Sol se convirtiera en un agujero negro, su horizonte de sucesos mediría solo unos 6 km de diámetro. El de la Tierra tendría el tamaño de una canica.

deep.x: A black hole's event horizon is surprisingly small for its mass. Squeeze any mass into a small enough sphere and it becomes a black hole.
Density isn't extreme for giants
The average density inside the horizon falls as mass grows. A supermassive black hole of a billion Suns has an average "density" inside its horizon lower than water.

items: average density can be below water's

deep.x: Mass, spin, charge
Physicists say "black holes have no hair": a black hole is fully described by just three numbers: mass, spin and electric charge. All other details of what fell in are hidden.
Spinning black holes drag spacetime around with them, so close in, nothing can stay still relative to distant stars.

cards.title: Agujeros negros supermasivos
cards.text: Casi todas las galaxias grandes tienen un agujero negro supermasivo en el centro. El nuestro, Sagitario A*, tiene unos 4 millones de veces la masa del Sol.

deep.x: Nearly every large galaxy hosts a central black hole of millions to billions of solar masses. Their masses correlate with their galaxies' bulges, suggesting they grow together.
Quasars

When a supermassive black hole swallows gas rapidly, the surrounding disc heats up and outshines its entire galaxy, sometimes thousands of times over. These are quasars, the brightest steady objects in the universe.
Jets
Magnetic fields near spinning black holes launch jets of particles at nearly light speed, extending hundreds of thousands of light-years. M87's jet is visible in ordinary telescopes.
A puzzle
Webb has found supermassive black holes already existing less than a billion years after the Big Bang. How they grew so big so fast is an active question.
Our own Sgr A* is quiet, eating very little, which is lucky for life in the galaxy.

cards.title: Espaguetización
cards.text: Cerca de un agujero negro pequeño, la gravedad tira mucho más de tus pies que de tu cabeza y te estira como un espagueti.

deep.x: Gravity's pull weakens with distance, so near a black hole the pull on your feet can be much stronger than on your head. This difference, a tidal force, stretches you lengthwise and squeezes you sideways.
Size matters, oddly

Tidal forces at the horizon are strongest for small black holes. Near a stellar black hole, you'd be torn apart long before reaching the horizon. A supermassive black hole's horizon is so big that you could cross it intact and only be spaghettified later.
Tidal disruption events
When a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole, it's shredded. About half its gas falls in and flares brightly for months. Telescopes catch dozens of these events.
Earth's tides are the same effect, much gentler: the Moon pulls the near side of the oceans more than the far side.

cards.title: El tiempo se ralentiza
cards.text: Cerca de un agujero negro, el tiempo pasa más despacio que lejos de él. Para un observador lejano, algo que cae parece congelarse en el borde.

deep.x: General relativity says time passes more slowly in stronger gravity. Near a black hole, the effect becomes extreme. A distant observer watching someone fall in sees their clock slow down and their image redden and fade as they approach the horizon, never quite seeming to cross.

items: sees the faller freeze and fade

deep.x: Interstellar's water planet
In the film *Interstellar*, physicist Kip Thorne helped calculate a planet near a giant spinning black hole where 1 hour equals 7 years on Earth. It's an extreme but physically inspired scenario.

v.unit: time passing elsewhere per hour on the planet

deep.x: Real measurements
Near Sgr A*, astronomers tracked the star S2 passing close in 2018 and measured its light being stretched by gravity, exactly as relativity predicts.
Even Earth's gravity slows time measurably: GPS clocks would drift without correcting for it.

cards.title: Ver lo invisible
cards.text: Los agujeros negros se descubren por sus efectos: estrellas que orbitan algo invisible, gas caliente y brillante que gira a su alrededor y ondulaciones en el espacio-tiempo.

deep.x: Black holes emit no light, but their surroundings do. Astronomers find them through the effects of their gravity on matter and light around them.
Stars around Sgr A*

For decades, teams led by Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez tracked stars orbiting an invisible point at the Milky Way's centre. The star S2 orbits every 16 years, at up to 2.5% of light speed. Their work won the 2020 Nobel Prize.
X-ray binaries
When a black hole orbits a normal star, it can pull gas off it. The gas heats to millions of degrees as it spirals in, glowing in X-rays.
Lone black holes
In 2022 astronomers detected an isolated black hole wandering through the galaxy by the way it briefly magnified a background star: microlensing.

steps: Black hole passes in front of a star

deep.x: The Milky Way may contain around 100 million stellar black holes, most of them invisible.

cards.title: Ondas gravitacionales

events.l: primera imagen de un agujero negro

cards.text: En 2015, los detectores LIGO captaron ondulaciones en el espacio-tiempo de dos agujeros negros que se fusionaron a 1300 millones de años luz, tal como Einstein había predicho un siglo antes.

deep.x: Accelerating masses create ripples in spacetime that travel at light speed, stretching and squeezing space as they pass. Einstein predicted them in 1916 but doubted they'd ever be detected: the effect is incredibly small.

steps: Stretch detectors by a fraction of a proton

deep.x: LIGO

Each LIGO detector has two 4 km arms at right angles. Lasers measure the arm lengths; a passing wave changes them by less than 1/10,000 of a proton's width. On 14 September 2015 both LIGO sites detected GW150914: two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging 1.3 billion light-years away.

items.l: solar masses turned into wave energy

deep.x: A new kind of astronomy

Since then, hundreds of mergers have been detected by LIGO, Virgo in Italy and KAGRA in Japan. In 2017 a neutron star merger was seen both in gravitational waves and in light, confirming that such collisions make gold.

events.l: indirect evidence from a binary pulsar
Nobel Prize and neutron star merger

deep.x: Turned into sound
The signal's frequency rises as the black holes spiral in, producing a "chirp" when converted to audio.
The 2015 merger briefly released more power in gravitational waves than all the stars in the observable universe combined emitted as light.

cards.title: La primera imagen
cards.text: En 2019, el Event Horizon Telescope, que une radiotelescopios de todo el mundo en un telescopio del tamaño de la Tierra, captó la sombra del agujero negro de M87. Sagitario A* llegó en 2022.

deep.x: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) linked radio observatories in Hawaii, Arizona, Mexico, Chile, Spain, the South Pole and elsewhere. Observing together at a 1.3 mm wavelength, they formed a virtual dish the size of Earth, sharp enough to read a newspaper in New York from Paris.

Released on 10 April 2019, the image showed a bright ring of hot gas around a dark shadow: the black hole at the centre of galaxy M87. The ring's size matched Einstein's predictions for a 6.5-billion-Sun black hole.
Sgr A* in 2022

Our own black hole, though much closer, was harder to image because gas around it changes in minutes. The 2022 image showed a similar ring, confirming the physics scales from millions to billions of Suns.
The data was too large to send over the internet: about 5 petabytes, so hard drives were physically shipped.

cards.title: Radiación de Hawking
cards.text: Stephen Hawking calculó en 1974 que los agujeros negros deberían perder energía poco a poco y acabar evaporándose, aunque en los reales eso tarda muchísimo más que la edad del universo.

deep.x: In 1974 Stephen Hawking combined quantum theory with general relativity and found that black holes aren't completely black: they should emit faint radiation and slowly lose mass. The smaller the black hole, the hotter it is and the faster it evaporates.
How faint?

A black hole the mass of the Sun would have a temperature of about 60 billionths of a degree above absolute zero, far colder than the cosmic microwave background, so for now it absorbs more than it emits.

items.a: Age of the universe so far

deep.x: The information paradox

If a black hole evaporates into random radiation, what happens to the information about what fell in? Quantum theory says information can't be destroyed. This puzzle remains one of the deepest in physics.
Never observed
Hawking radiation from real black holes is far too faint to detect. Physicists have seen analogous effects in lab systems with sound waves in fluids, called "dumb holes".
Hawking's gravestone in Westminster Abbey is engraved with his formula for black hole temperature.

quiz.q: ¿Qué es el horizonte de sucesos?
quiz.explain: Desde dentro no escapa ni la luz.

quiz.q: ¿Qué detectó LIGO en 2015?
quiz.explain: De la fusión de dos agujeros negros.

lessons.title: Telescopios y luz
lessons.summary: Cómo vemos el universo invisible.

cards.title: Mirar al pasado
cards.text: La luz tarda en viajar, así que vemos la Luna como era hace 1,3 segundos, el Sol hace 8 minutos y Andrómeda hace 2,5 millones de años.

deep.x: Light travels at 300,000 km/s: fast, but not infinitely fast. Everything we see is a message from the past, delayed by the distance it travelled. The farther we look, the older the light.
A time machine for astronomers

Because distant light is old, telescopes can watch the universe's history directly. Webb sees galaxies as they were less than 400 million years after the Big Bang, when the universe was about 3% of its current age.

steps: Distant galaxies: billions of years ago
Cosmic microwave background: 380,000 years after the Big Bang

deep.x: Is that star still there?

For most stars you see, the light left them decades to centuries ago. Stars live millions to billions of years, so almost all are still there; but for a few distant massive stars, we might be seeing a star that has already exploded.

deep.w: Many stars we see are already dead
deep.r: Most naked-eye stars are within a few hundred light-years and still shining

deep.x: Looking out is looking back: the deepest images are also the oldest photographs ever taken.

cards.title: El telescopio de Galileo
cards.text: En 1609–10, Galileo apuntó un sencillo telescopio al cielo y vio las lunas de Júpiter, las fases de Venus, las manchas solares e innumerables estrellas en la Vía Láctea.

deep.x: Galileo didn't invent the telescope; Dutch spectacle makers did in 1608. Hearing about it, he built his own, improving it to about 20× magnification, and was the first to point one systematically at the sky.
What he saw

x: **Mountains and craters on the Moon**: it wasn't a perfect heavenly sphere
**Four moons of Jupiter**: proof that not everything orbits Earth
**Phases of Venus**: only possible if Venus orbits the Sun
**Countless stars in the Milky Way**: the universe was bigger than anyone thought

deep.x: Why it was explosive
The phases of Venus in particular contradicted Ptolemy's Earth-centred model. Galileo's support for Copernicus led to his trial by the Inquisition in 1633 and house arrest for the rest of his life.
Galileo's best telescope had a field of view so narrow he could see only a quarter of the full Moon at once.

cards.title: Refractores y reflectores
cards.text: Los telescopios refractores usan lentes; los reflectores, inventados por Newton, usan espejos curvos. Todos los grandes telescopios de investigación son reflectores, porque los espejos pueden hacerse enormes.

deep.x: A refractor bends light with a big lens at the front; a reflector collects light with a curved mirror at the back. Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668 to avoid the coloured fringes that early lenses produced.
Why lenses hit a limit

A lens can only be supported at its edge, so big ones sag under their own weight, and light must pass through flawless glass. The largest refractor ever, at Yerkes Observatory (1897), has a 1-metre lens. Mirrors can be supported from behind, segmented and made enormous.
Modern tricks

x: **Segmented mirrors**: many hexagons acting as one, as on Keck and Webb
**Adaptive optics**: deformable mirrors that cancel atmospheric blur hundreds of times a second
**Interferometry**: combining several telescopes to sharpen detail

deep.x: For backyard astronomy, a simple reflector (a "Dobsonian") gives the most light-gathering power per euro.

cards.title: Cuanto más grande, mejor
cards.text: La capacidad de un telescopio para captar luz depende de la superficie de su espejo. El futuro Extremely Large Telescope, en Chile, tiene un espejo de 39 m.

deep.x: A telescope's light-gathering power grows with the area of its mirror, which goes with the diameter squared. Double the diameter and you collect four times as much light, seeing fainter, more distant objects.
Sharper too
Bigger mirrors also resolve finer detail, though on the ground the atmosphere blurs the view unless adaptive optics correct it.
The Extremely Large Telescope

ESO's ELT in Chile's Atacama Desert will have a 39 m mirror made of 798 hexagonal segments, collecting more light than all today's large research telescopes combined. Portugal is an ESO member and contributes to its instruments.
The ELT's dome is about 80 m tall, almost as high as the Torre dos Clérigos in Porto (76 m).

cards.title: El espectro electromagnético
cards.text: La luz visible es una porción diminuta del espectro. Cada longitud de onda revela cosas distintas, desde el polvo frío en radio hasta las estrellas que explotan en rayos X.

deep.x: Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields. Visible light, wavelengths of about 400–700 nanometres, is a sliver of a much larger spectrum, from radio waves metres long to gamma rays smaller than an atom.
What each reveals

items.b: cold gas, pulsars, black hole jets

deep.x: Energy and wavelength
Shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon. That's why UV burns skin and X-rays pass through it, while radio waves pass harmlessly through your body all day.
Multi-wavelength astronomy
The same object looks completely different across the spectrum. The Crab Nebula glows in radio, infrared, visible, X-ray and gamma rays, each revealing a different process.
Your eyes evolved for visible light because that's where the Sun is brightest and where Earth's atmosphere is transparent.

cards.title: Infrarrojo

steps: Una galaxia joven emite luz visible
La luz se estira al infrarrojo

cards.text: La luz infrarroja atraviesa las nubes de polvo y muestra objetos fríos. El James Webb observa en infrarrojo para detectar estrellas recién nacidas y las primeras galaxias, cuya luz se estiró con la expansión.

deep.x: Infrared is light with wavelengths a bit longer than red, felt as heat. Everything warm glows in infrared, including you. Infrared also slips through dust clouds that block visible light, revealing stars being born inside them.

items: shows cool objects and newborn stars

deep.x: Redshift pushes light into infrared

As the universe expands, light from distant galaxies is stretched. Ultraviolet and visible light emitted 13 billion years ago arrives today as infrared. To see the first galaxies, you need an infrared telescope.

steps: Young galaxy emits UV and visible light

deep.x: Why Webb is so cold

An infrared telescope must be colder than what it observes, or its own heat drowns the signal. Webb sits 1.5 million km away, shielded by a five-layer sunshield, at about −233 °C; one instrument is cooled further to −266 °C.
Herschel discovered infrared in 1800 by putting thermometers beyond the red end of a rainbow from a prism and finding it was warmest there.

cards.title: ¿Por qué ir al espacio?
cards.text: La atmósfera terrestre emborrona la luz de las estrellas y bloquea los rayos X, el UV y gran parte del infrarrojo. Los telescopios espaciales evitan ambos problemas.

deep.x: Earth's atmosphere does three annoying things to astronomers: it shimmers (making stars twinkle and images blurry), it glows faintly, and it blocks whole parts of the spectrum.

items: Absorption: blocks X-rays, UV, much infrared

deep.x: What gets through

Only visible light, some infrared and radio reach the ground well. Ozone blocks UV; water vapour blocks much infrared; X-rays and gamma rays are absorbed high up. That's lucky for life, but bad for astronomy.
Ground strikes back

Space telescopes are expensive and hard to repair. Ground telescopes can be much bigger and upgraded easily, and adaptive optics now remove much of the blur. The best sites are high and dry: Chile's Atacama, Hawaii's Mauna Kea, La Palma in the Canaries.
Modern astronomy needs both: space telescopes for sharpness and invisible wavelengths, ground giants for light-gathering power.

cards.title: Radiotelescopios
cards.text: Los radiotelescopios son antenas gigantes. Al unir antenas de distintos continentes se crea un telescopio virtual tan ancho como la distancia entre ellas.

deep.x: Radio waves from space are incredibly faint: all the radio energy ever collected by radio telescopes is less than the energy of a falling snowflake. Huge dishes are needed to gather enough.
History
Karl Jansky discovered radio waves from the Milky Way's centre in 1932 while studying static for Bell Labs. Radio astronomy then found quasars, pulsars and the cosmic microwave background.
Arrays

By combining dishes far apart, astronomers get the sharpness of one telescope as wide as the distance between them. The Event Horizon Telescope linked dishes across the world into an Earth-sized virtual telescope.

items.b: thousands of antennas, South Africa and Australia

deep.x: Protecting radio quiet
Phones, Wi-Fi and satellites cause interference, so radio telescopes are built in remote "radio quiet zones".
Portugal participates in the Square Kilometre Array, the largest radio telescope project in the world.

cards.title: Espectroscopia
cards.text: Al descomponer la luz de una estrella en un arcoíris aparecen líneas oscuras: las huellas de los elementos de la estrella. Así sabemos de qué están hechas las estrellas sin visitarlas.

deep.x: Pass starlight through a prism or grating and it spreads into a rainbow, a spectrum. Atoms of each element absorb light at exact, unique wavelengths, leaving dark lines like a barcode. Matching barcodes reveals what a star is made of.
Helium was found in the Sun first
In 1868, astronomers saw an unknown yellow line in the Sun's spectrum during an eclipse. They named the element helium, after Helios, the Sun. It wasn't found on Earth until 1895.

events.l: Kirchhoff and Bunsen link lines to elements

deep.x: Much more than ingredients
Philosopher's challenge
In 1835 philosopher Auguste Comte said we would never know the chemical composition of stars. Within 25 years, spectroscopy proved him wrong.
Spectroscopy also finds exoplanets (by the star's wobble) and measures the universe's expansion (by redshift).

cards.title: Cielos oscuros
cards.text: La contaminación lumínica oculta la mayoría de las estrellas a quien vive en la ciudad. La reserva Dark Sky Alqueva, en Portugal, fue el primer «Destino Turístico Starlight» del mundo, certificado en 2011.

deep.x: Artificial light at night scatters in the atmosphere and creates skyglow that hides stars. About 80% of the world's population, and more than 99% of people in Europe and the USA, live under light-polluted skies. Most Europeans can't see the Milky Way from home.
Not just astronomy

x: Birds migrating at night are disoriented, and many die hitting lit buildings
Sea turtle hatchlings head towards lights instead of the sea
Insects die around lamps, contributing to insect decline
Night light can disrupt human sleep and hormones

deep.x: Simple fixes

items: Use only the light you need

deep.x: Dark Sky Alqueva

Around the Alqueva lake in the Alentejo, municipalities controlled lighting to protect the night sky. In 2011 it became the world's first Starlight Tourism Destination, with an observatory and stargazing tours.
On a truly dark night you can see around 4,000 stars at once; in central Lisbon, perhaps a few dozen.

quiz.q: ¿Por qué vemos Andrómeda como era hace 2,5 millones de años?
options: Su luz tardó eso en llegarnos
quiz.explain: La luz viaja a una velocidad finita.

quiz.q: ¿Cómo sabemos de qué están hechas las estrellas?
quiz.explain: Cada elemento deja una huella.

quiz.q: ¿Por qué el Webb observa en infrarrojo?
options: La luz de las primeras galaxias se estira hasta el infrarrojo
quiz.explain: La expansión cósmica estira la luz.

lessons.title: Gravedad y órbitas
lessons.summary: Por qué las cosas caen, y por qué la Luna no.

cards.title: La gravedad de Newton
cards.text: Isaac Newton se dio cuenta de que la fuerza que hace caer una manzana es la misma que mantiene a la Luna en órbita. Toda masa atrae a cualquier otra masa.

deep.x: In 1687 Newton published his law of universal gravitation: every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to both masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The same law explains falling apples, tides and planetary orbits.
Gravity is weak

G is tiny, so gravity between everyday objects is minuscule. Two people standing 1 m apart attract with a force less than a millionth of a newton. Gravity only dominates because planets and stars are enormous and it never cancels out, unlike electric charges.
Weighing the Earth
In 1798 Henry Cavendish measured G with a delicate torsion balance in his shed, which let scientists calculate Earth's mass: about 6 × 10²⁴ kg.
Where Newton falls short
Newton's law is superb for spacecraft navigation, but it couldn't explain a small drift in Mercury's orbit. Einstein's general relativity (1915) did.
The apple story is probably partly true: Newton told friends that a falling apple in his family garden set him thinking about gravity.

cards.title: La ley de la inversa del cuadrado
cards.text: Si duplicas la distancia, la gravedad baja a una cuarta parte. Si la triplicas, baja a una novena parte.

deep.x: Gravity spreads out in all directions, like light from a bulb. At twice the distance, the same influence covers four times the area, so it's four times weaker. Many things follow this rule: light, sound and electric force.
Gravity with height
Because Earth's centre is 6,371 km below your feet, going up a few hundred kilometres changes gravity only a little. At the ISS (400 km), it's still about 89% as strong.
Light works the same way
A star twice as far away appears four times dimmer. Astronomers use this to estimate distances to stars whose true brightness they know.
Inverse-square laws appear whenever something spreads evenly from a point into three-dimensional space.

cards.title: Orbitar es caer

steps: Bastante rápido: cae alrededor de la Tierra

cards.text: Una nave en órbita cae constantemente hacia la Tierra, pero avanza de lado tan rápido que el suelo se curva bajo ella. Newton imaginó un cañón en lo alto de una montaña.

deep.x: In his *Principia*, Newton drew a cannon on a very tall mountain. Each faster shot lands farther away; at the right speed, the ball falls towards Earth but the curved surface drops away just as fast, and it circles forever.

steps: Faster still: elliptical orbit or escape

deep.x: Speed depends on height
Lower orbits need higher speeds and are quicker. The ISS at 400 km circles in 92 minutes; the Moon, 384,000 km away, takes 27 days.
Orbital oddities

x: To catch up with something ahead in orbit, you slow down, drop to a lower, faster orbit, then rise again
Speeding up raises your orbit, which makes you slower overall
A dropped spanner keeps orbiting alongside the astronaut who dropped it

deep.x: In orbit you're not floating above gravity; you're falling continually and always missing the ground.

cards.title: Ingravidez

items.r: Hay ~90 % de gravedad: están en caída libre

cards.text: Los astronautas de la ISS se sienten ingrávidos no porque no haya gravedad, que allí es un 90 % de la de la superficie, sino porque caen junto con la estación.

deep.x: Weight is the feeling of the floor pushing up on you. In a freely falling lift, the floor would fall with you and you'd float. Astronauts in orbit are in permanent free fall along with their station, so nothing pushes on anything: weightlessness.

deep.w: There's no gravity in space
deep.r: At the ISS, gravity is about 89% as strong as on the ground

deep.x: Feeling it on Earth

x: The stomach "drop" at the top of a roller-coaster hill is a moment of free fall
Parabolic flights (the "vomit comet") give about 20–25 seconds of weightlessness per arc
Drop towers give a few seconds for experiments

deep.x: Microgravity
Scientists say "microgravity" because tiny forces remain: air drag, crew moving, the station's rotation. Flames burn as round blue spheres, and water forms floating balls.
Astronauts feel briefly heavy after landing; some have dropped cups, forgetting objects now fall.

cards.title: Masa y peso
cards.text: Tu masa es la misma en todas partes; tu peso depende de la gravedad. Una persona de 70 kg pesaría en la Luna más o menos como 12 kg en la Tierra.

deep.x: Mass is how much matter you contain, measured in kilograms; it's the same anywhere in the universe. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons. Bathroom scales show "kilograms", but they really measure force and assume Earth's gravity.
Same you, different worlds

v.unit: weight of a 70 kg person, newtons

deep.x: Mass still matters in space

Even weightless, mass resists acceleration: pushing a heavy object in orbit is hard to start and hard to stop. Astronauts measure their body mass with a spring chair that oscillates; heavier people bounce more slowly.
Gravity varies slightly over Earth: you weigh about 0.5% less at the equator than at the poles, due to Earth's spin and bulge.

cards.title: Las leyes de Kepler
cards.text: Johannes Kepler descubrió que los planetas se mueven en elipses, barren áreas iguales en tiempos iguales y que los planetas más lejanos tardan más en completar su órbita.

deep.x: Using Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars, Johannes Kepler found three laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1619, decades before Newton explained why they work.

items: First law: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus
Second law: a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times

deep.x: The second law in action

A planet speeds up when close to the Sun and slows when far. Earth moves fastest in early January, at perihelion, about 30.3 km/s, and slowest in early July, about 29.3 km/s. That's partly why northern winter is a few days shorter than summer.
The third law
The square of a planet's year is proportional to the cube of its distance. In units of Earth years and AU, period² = distance³ exactly.

x: Jupiter: 5.2 AU

deep.x: Kepler's third law is used today to weigh stars and black holes from the orbits around them.

cards.title: Velocidad de escape
cards.text: Para escapar por completo de la gravedad de la Tierra, necesitarías unos 11,2 km/s. En la Luna, solo 2,4 km/s.

deep.x: Escape velocity is the speed needed to coast away from a body forever without further thrust, ignoring air resistance. It depends on the body's mass and radius, not on the mass of the object escaping.
Around the Solar System
Rockets don't need it all at once

Escape velocity applies to a cannonball fired once. Rockets keep firing their engines as they climb, so they can leave gradually. Still, to leave Earth for good, a spacecraft must eventually gain that much energy.
Escaping the Sun
From Earth's orbit, escaping the Sun requires about 42 km/s, but Earth already moves at 30 km/s, so probes need "only" about 12 km/s extra in the right direction.
A black hole is an object whose escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.

cards.title: Asistencias gravitatorias
cards.text: Las naves pasan rozando los planetas para robarles un poco de su velocidad orbital, como una pelota que rebota en un tren en marcha. Las Voyager usaron así Júpiter y Saturno.

deep.x: A spacecraft flying close behind a moving planet gets pulled along and leaves faster, relative to the Sun. The planet loses an immeasurably tiny bit of orbital speed in exchange. Flying in front of a planet does the opposite and slows the craft down.
The train analogy
Throw a tennis ball at an approaching train: it bounces back faster than you threw it, having picked up the train's speed. The planet is the train; gravity is the bounce.
Famous slingshots

x: Voyager 2 used Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus to reach Neptune in 12 years instead of 30
Parker Solar Probe used Venus seven times to slow down and fall towards the Sun
Rosetta used Earth three times and Mars once to catch a comet

deep.x: Discovered by a student
In 1961 UCLA student Michael Minovitch used computers to calculate gravity-assist trajectories, showing they could make outer-planet missions practical.
Gravity assists are free fuel: they let small spacecraft reach places their rockets alone never could.

cards.title: Puntos de Lagrange

items.b: entre el Sol y la Tierra, observatorios solares
más allá de la Tierra, Webb

cards.text: Hay cinco puntos donde un objeto pequeño puede mantener su posición respecto a dos cuerpos grandes. El Webb está en L2, a 1,5 millones de km de la Tierra, en el lado opuesto al Sol.

deep.x: Around any two orbiting bodies, like the Sun and Earth, there are five points where gravity and orbital motion balance, so a small spacecraft can stay in the same position relative to both. Joseph-Louis Lagrange worked them out in 1772.

items.b: 1.5 million km sunward, SOHO watches the Sun
1.5 million km outward, Webb and Gaia

deep.x: Stable and unstable

L1, L2 and L3 are like balancing on a hilltop: spacecraft need small engine burns every few weeks to stay. L4 and L5 are like valleys: objects naturally collect there. Jupiter has thousands of "Trojan" asteroids at its L4 and L5 points.
Why L2 for Webb
At L2, the Sun, Earth and Moon are all on one side, so a single sunshield blocks them all, keeping the telescope cold. And it stays in constant contact with Earth.
NASA's Lucy mission, launched in 2021, is touring Jupiter's Trojan asteroids, named after heroes of the Trojan War.

cards.title: Órbita geoestacionaria
cards.text: A unos 36 000 km de altura, un satélite da una vuelta al día y se queda sobre el mismo punto. Por eso las antenas parabólicas de TV apuntan a un punto fijo del cielo.

deep.x: At 35,786 km above the equator, an orbit takes exactly one sidereal day. A satellite there moves as fast as Earth turns beneath it, appearing fixed in the sky. Science-fiction author Arthur C. Clarke popularised the idea for communications in 1945.
Uses

x: TV broadcasting: dishes can be fixed in one direction
Weather satellites watching the same half of Earth continuously, like Meteosat for Europe
Some communications and military satellites

deep.x: Downsides
The great distance means a radio delay of about 0.25 s for a round trip: noticeable on phone calls and online games. And geostationary satellites can't see the polar regions well.
A crowded ring
There's only one geostationary ring, so slots are allocated by the International Telecommunication Union. Old satellites are boosted a few hundred km higher into a "graveyard orbit".
In Portugal, satellite TV dishes point roughly south, about 40° up, towards satellites above the equator.

quiz.q: ¿Por qué los astronautas de la ISS no sienten su peso?
options: Están en caída libre con la estación
quiz.explain: La gravedad sigue siendo un 90 % de la de la superficie.

quiz.q: Si duplicas la distancia, la gravedad pasa a ser…
quiz.explain: La ley de la inversa del cuadrado.

lessons.title: El tiempo, el espacio y Einstein
lessons.summary: La relatividad sin deberes de matemáticas.

cards.title: La velocidad de la luz

items.l: vueltas a la Tierra por segundo

cards.text: La luz viaja a unos 300 000 km por segundo en el vacío, y todos los observadores miden la misma velocidad, por rápido que se muevan. Ese hecho tan simple lo cambia todo.

deep.x: In 1887 Michelson and Morley expected the speed of light to vary with Earth's motion through space; it didn't. In 1905, Einstein took this as a principle: light in a vacuum always moves at the same speed, c, for every observer, however fast they're moving.
Why that's strange

If you throw a ball forwards from a moving train, its speed adds to the train's. But shine a torch forwards from a rocket at half light speed, and both you and a watcher on the ground measure the light at exactly c. For that to work, time and space themselves must adjust.
Defining the metre
Since 1983 the speed of light has been fixed by definition, and the metre is defined as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

x: Light takes 1.3 s to reach the Moon and about 0.13 s to circle Earth
In glass or water, light slows, but c in a vacuum is the universal limit

deep.x: c isn't really about light: it's the speed limit of cause and effect in the universe.

cards.title: Dilatación del tiempo
cards.text: Los relojes en movimiento van más lentos. Un astronauta que viajara casi a la velocidad de la luz descubriría al volver que en la Tierra ha pasado más tiempo que para él.

deep.x: If light's speed is the same for everyone, moving clocks must tick slowly from the point of view of someone watching them pass. The effect is tiny at everyday speeds and huge near light speed.
How big?
Evidence

x: **Muons**: particles made high in the atmosphere live only 2.2 microseconds, too short to reach the ground, yet many do, because their clocks run slow at 99.9% of c
**Atomic clocks on planes** (Hafele–Keating, 1971) showed the predicted tiny differences
**Particle accelerators** see fast unstable particles live longer exactly as predicted

deep.w: Time dilation is just a clock error
deep.r: Every process slows, including ageing; time itself runs differently

deep.x: Astronauts on the ISS age about 0.01 seconds less than us over six months.

cards.title: La paradoja de los gemelos
cards.text: Un gemelo viaja a una estrella al 87 % de la velocidad de la luz y vuelve; el otro se queda en casa. Al regresar, el viajero ha envejecido más o menos la mitad. La dilatación del tiempo se ha confirmado con relojes atómicos a bordo de aviones.

deep.x: Twin A stays on Earth; twin B flies to a star 10 light-years away at 87% of c and returns. Earth clocks show about 23 years; B's ship clocks show about 11.5 years. B comes back younger.
Why is it a "paradox"?

From B's view, Earth moved away and back, so shouldn't A be younger? The situations aren't symmetric: B accelerates, turns around and decelerates, switching reference frames. A stays in one frame the whole time. Calculations from either side agree: the traveller ages less.
A one-way ticket to the future
Time dilation makes travel to the future possible in principle: go fast enough and you return to a distant future. Travel to the past is a different matter, with no known way to do it.
Cosmonaut Gennady Padalka, after 879 days in orbit, is about 0.02 seconds younger than if he'd stayed on Earth.

cards.title: Contracción de la longitud
cards.text: Los objetos que se mueven muy rápido son más cortos en la dirección de su movimiento, según los mide alguien que los ve pasar. Solo se nota cerca de la velocidad de la luz.

deep.x: Objects moving fast are measured as shorter along their direction of motion by an observer they're passing. A spaceship flying at 87% of c would appear half as long as it is at rest.
Hand in hand with time dilation

The muon example shows both views: from the ground, the muon's clock runs slow; from the muon's view, the atmosphere is squashed thin, so it reaches the ground in time. Both descriptions agree on the result.
What it doesn't do

x: It doesn't squash objects physically; it's about measurements between frames
The traveller notices nothing odd on their own ship
At everyday speeds it's far too small to measure

deep.x: Very fast objects would actually look rotated rather than squashed in photos, an effect called Terrell rotation, because light from different parts takes different times to reach the camera.

cards.title: E = mc²

items.m: velocidad de la luz al cuadrado, un número enorme

cards.text: La masa y la energía son dos formas de lo mismo. Una cantidad diminuta de masa encierra una energía enorme, que es lo que alimenta el Sol y los reactores nucleares.

deep.x: Published by Einstein in 1905 as a follow-up to special relativity, E = mc² says mass and energy are equivalent. Because c² is huge (9 × 10¹⁶), a tiny bit of mass is equivalent to a vast amount of energy.

x: 1 gram of mass
= 9 × 10¹³ joules ≈ 25 million kWh

deep.x: Where it shows up

x: **The Sun**: converts about 4 million tonnes of mass to energy each second
**Nuclear power**: splitting uranium releases energy as products weigh slightly less
**Particle physics**: collisions turn energy into new particles of matter

deep.x: A common misunderstanding
E = mc² doesn't mean things easily turn into energy. In fission only about 0.1% of the mass is converted; in fusion about 0.7%. Total conversion happens only when matter meets antimatter.
Even chemistry
When you burn wood, the products weigh very slightly less than the wood and oxygen did, but the difference is far too small to measure.
A paperclip's worth of mass (1 g), fully converted, would supply the electricity of a Portuguese town of about 5,000 people for a year.

cards.title: La gravedad curva el espacio-tiempo
cards.text: En la relatividad general (1915), la masa curva el espacio-tiempo y los objetos siguen esas curvas. Piensa en una bola pesada sobre una cama elástica que hace rodar canicas hacia ella.

deep.x: In 1915 Einstein's general relativity replaced Newton's force of gravity with geometry: mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects move along the straightest possible paths through that curved spacetime. "Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve," as John Wheeler put it.
The trampoline picture
A heavy ball on a trampoline makes a dip; marbles roll towards it. It's a helpful image but imperfect: in real spacetime, time itself is curved too, which is what mostly makes things fall.
Predictions confirmed
Gravity slows time
Clocks run slower in stronger gravity. A clock at sea level runs slightly slower than one at the top of a mountain. Modern atomic clocks detect the difference over just 1 cm of height.
Your head ages slightly faster than your feet, about 90 billionths of a second over a lifetime.

cards.title: La luz se curva
cards.text: En 1919, Arthur Eddington midió cómo la luz de las estrellas se curvaba alrededor del Sol durante un eclipse, justo como había predicho Einstein. Aquello lo hizo famoso en todo el mundo.

deep.x: If gravity curves spacetime, light passing a massive object should bend. Einstein predicted that starlight grazing the Sun would shift by 1.75 arcseconds, twice what a Newtonian calculation gave.
The 1919 eclipse

Stars near the Sun are normally hidden by its glare, so Arthur Eddington organised expeditions to photograph them during the total eclipse of 29 May 1919: one to Sobral in Brazil and one to Príncipe, then a Portuguese colony off Africa. Their measurements favoured Einstein.
Overnight fame
On 7 November 1919, *The Times* headline read "Revolution in Science". Einstein became a global celebrity almost overnight.

x: The Príncipe expedition is commemorated in São Tomé and Príncipe and in Portuguese science history
Later radio measurements confirmed the bending to better than 0.01%

deep.x: Eddington's team was nearly clouded out on Príncipe; the clouds cleared only partly during totality.

cards.title: El GPS necesita la relatividad
cards.text: Los relojes de los satélites GPS adelantan unos 38 microsegundos al día: van más rápido por la menor gravedad y más lento por su velocidad. Sin correcciones, las posiciones se desviarían kilómetros cada día.

deep.x: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks and orbit at 20,200 km, moving at about 14,000 km/h. Two relativistic effects change their clocks' rates compared with clocks on the ground.

items.b: speed slows the clocks by ~7 µs a day
weaker gravity speeds them by ~45 µs a day

deep.x: Why microseconds matter

GPS works by timing signals that travel at light speed. A timing error of 1 microsecond means a position error of about 300 m. Uncorrected, 38 µs a day would accumulate into errors of around 10 km a day.
The fix
Engineers set satellite clocks to tick slightly slower before launch, at 10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23 MHz, so that in orbit they match ground time.
Every time your phone finds your location, it's quietly confirming Einstein.

cards.title: Lentes gravitacionales

steps: La luz pasa junto a un gran cúmulo

cards.text: Los cúmulos de galaxias muy masivos curvan la luz de las galaxias que hay detrás y crean arcos e imágenes múltiples. Los astrónomos usan estas lupas naturales.

deep.x: Massive objects bend light from things behind them, acting as cosmic lenses. A galaxy cluster can magnify, distort and multiply the image of a distant galaxy into arcs or even a complete ring.

items: Weak: slight distortions, mapping dark matter

deep.x: Einstein rings
When source, lens and observer line up perfectly, the background galaxy appears as a ring around the lens. Webb and Hubble have imaged many.
Uses

x: **Natural telescopes**: lensing magnifies faint early galaxies Webb couldn't otherwise see
**Dark matter maps**: lensing reveals mass we can't see
**Finding exoplanets**: a star passing in front of another briefly brightens it; a planet adds a tell-tale blip

deep.x: A lensed supernova, "Refsdal", appeared four times around a galaxy in 2014, and astronomers correctly predicted a fifth image would appear about a year later.

cards.title: Nada más rápido que la luz

viz.unit: % de la velocidad de la luz

cards.text: Nada con masa puede alcanzar la velocidad de la luz: cuanto más te acercas, más energía cuesta cada poquito de velocidad extra. La información tampoco puede viajar más rápido que la luz.

deep.x: As an object with mass speeds up, the energy needed to accelerate it further rises without limit as it approaches c. Reaching light speed would take infinite energy, so particles with mass can only get closer and closer.
Fastest so far

x: The LHC accelerates protons to 99.9999991% of c
Parker Solar Probe, the fastest spacecraft, reached about 0.064% of c
Light itself has no mass, so it always travels at c

deep.x: Causality
If information could travel faster than light, some observers would see effects before their causes. Relativity's speed limit protects cause and effect.
Loopholes that aren't

items.b: space stretches, distant galaxies recede faster than c

deep.x: The universe's speed limit means the nearest stars, let alone other galaxies, will remain years to millions of years away, even for light.

quiz.q: ¿Qué le pasa a un reloj que se mueve muy rápido?
quiz.explain: Dilatación del tiempo.

quiz.q: ¿Por qué el GPS necesita la relatividad?
options: Los relojes de los satélites van a otro ritmo
quiz.explain: Sin corregir, el error crece kilómetros al día.

lessons.title: La vida de un astronauta
lessons.summary: Comer, dormir y trabajar en órbita.

cards.title: Hacerse astronauta
cards.text: Las agencias espaciales eligen a un puñado entre miles de candidatos. La selección de la ESA de 2022 recibió más de 22 500 solicitudes para 17 plazas, entre astronautas y reservas.
