deep.x: Agencies look for people who are healthy, calm under pressure, good team players and expert in something useful: medicine, engineering, science or flying. Candidates go through rounds of tests over more than a year.
Typical requirements (ESA)

x: A master's degree in science, engineering, medicine or maths, or test-pilot training
Several years of professional experience
Fluent English; other languages a plus
Height roughly 150–190 cm and good health; glasses are allowed

deep.x: Not just superhumans

Agencies stress teamwork and resilience more than athletic prowess. In 2022 ESA also selected John McFall, a Paralympic sprinter and surgeon, as the first "parastronaut" to study whether people with a physical disability can fly in space.
Portugal joined ESA in 2000, so Portuguese citizens can apply to ESA astronaut selections.

cards.title: Entrenamiento
cards.text: Los astronautas se entrenan durante años: paseos espaciales ensayados bajo el agua, entrenamiento de supervivencia, ruso, robótica y vuelos en aviones que crean breves momentos de ingravidez.

deep.x: Basic training takes about a year; mission-specific training can take two more. Astronauts must master the station's systems, science experiments, robotics and emergencies.
Underwater spacewalks

NASA's Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory is a pool 62 m long and 12 m deep holding a full-size ISS mock-up. Weighted suits make astronauts neither float nor sink, imitating weightlessness for six-hour sessions.
The skills list

items: Survival training in forest, sea and caves

deep.x: Expeditionary skills
ESA's CAVES programme sends astronauts underground for days to practise teamwork in isolation. Survival training covers landing off course in the wilderness, a real risk with capsules.
Much training is about failure: fire, depressurisation and toxic leaks are rehearsed until responses become automatic.
Astronauts learn to fly jets and keep flying them; NASA uses T-38 trainers to practise fast decision-making.

cards.title: Comer en el espacio
cards.text: La comida viene en bolsas y latas; las migas son peligrosas, así que las tortillas de trigo sustituyen al pan. En órbita el sentido del gusto se apaga, por eso a los astronautas les encantan las salsas picantes.

deep.x: Space food has come a long way from 1960s tubes of paste. ISS crews choose from about 200 items: thermostabilised, freeze-dried, irradiated and fresh fruit when cargo arrives.
Rules of the table

x: No crumbs: they float into eyes and equipment, so tortillas replace bread
Salt and pepper come as liquids
Food sticks to forks by surface tension; drinks are sipped from pouches
Fizzy drinks don't work well: gas and liquid don't separate in the stomach

deep.x: Taste changes
Fluid shifting to the head causes a "stuffy nose" feeling, dulling smell and taste. Astronauts often crave hot sauces and strong flavours.
Growing food
Astronauts have grown lettuce, radishes, chillies and flowers in the Veggie chamber. Future Mars missions will need much more home-grown food.
In 1965 astronaut John Young smuggled a corned-beef sandwich onto Gemini 3; its crumbs caused a fuss in Congress.

cards.title: Dormir
cards.text: Los astronautas duermen en cabinas pequeñas, en sacos de dormir sujetos a la pared. No hay «arriba», así que puedes dormir en cualquier orientación.

deep.x: Each ISS astronaut has a small private crew quarter, the size of a phone booth, with a sleeping bag strapped to the wall, a laptop and a light. Without gravity there's no need for a bed: you just float in the bag.

items: Sleeping bag tied to the wall
Eye mask for 16 sunrises a day

deep.x: Why ventilation matters
In weightlessness, warm breath doesn't rise. Exhaled CO₂ can pool around your face, causing headaches, so crew quarters need constant airflow.

steps: No convection to carry CO₂ away

deep.x: Sleep problems

x: Crews average about 6 hours a night, less than on Earth
16 sunrises a day disrupt the body clock, so lighting is tuned to mimic day and night
Some astronauts' arms float up in front of them while asleep

deep.x: Station "night" follows UTC (Greenwich time), so on the ISS everyone lives on London's clock, Portugal's winter time.

cards.title: El cuerpo en el espacio
cards.text: Sin gravedad, los músculos y los huesos se debilitan, los líquidos se desplazan hacia la cabeza y la columna se estira; los astronautas crecen unos 3 cm de forma temporal.

deep.x: Weightlessness affects nearly every body system. Without the constant load of gravity, the body adapts as if those muscles and bones aren't needed.
Puffy face, bird legs
About 2 litres of fluid shift from the legs to the upper body. Astronauts get puffy faces and thin "bird legs" in the first days.
Space adaptation
Over half of astronauts get space sickness during the first two or three days: nausea and disorientation as the brain reinterprets the inner ear's signals.
The Twin Study

In 2015–16 NASA compared astronaut Scott Kelly, who spent nearly a year in orbit, with his identical twin Mark on Earth. Most changes, in genes, immune system and microbes, returned to normal after landing; a few persisted.
Astronauts grow up to about 3 cm taller in orbit as their spine discs expand; they shrink back on return, sometimes with back pain.

cards.title: Ejercicio

items.l: hueso perdido al mes sin él

cards.text: Para combatir la pérdida de hueso y músculo, las tripulaciones de la ISS hacen unas dos horas de ejercicio al día en una cinta de correr con arneses, una bicicleta y una máquina de resistencia.

deep.x: Exercise is the main defence against bone and muscle loss. ISS crews exercise about 2 hours a day, six days a week, as part of their work schedule.

items.b: running in a harness pulling them down
resistance machine using vacuum cylinders, like lifting weights

deep.x: How the machines work

In weightlessness, free weights weigh nothing. The ARED resistance device uses vacuum cylinders to create up to about 270 kg of resistance for squats and deadlifts. Treadmills use bungee harnesses to pull runners onto the belt.
It works, partly
Modern exercise regimes have greatly reduced muscle loss and helped protect bone, though some bone loss still occurs. Diet with enough vitamin D and calories helps too.
These lessons help on Earth too: research on astronaut bones informs osteoporosis treatment.

cards.title: Reciclaje de agua
cards.text: En la ISS, cerca del 98 % del agua, incluidos el sudor y la orina, se recicla y se convierte en agua potable limpia.

deep.x: Water is heavy to launch, so the ISS recycles almost everything: urine, sweat, shower water and even moisture from the air. In 2023 its system reached 98% water recovery.
The "coffee" joke
Astronauts joke that "yesterday's coffee becomes today's coffee". The recycled water is cleaner than most tap water on Earth.
Air too

x: Oxygen is made by splitting water with electricity (electrolysis)
CO₂ is scrubbed from the air; some is combined with hydrogen to make more water
Trace gases are filtered to avoid build-up

deep.x: Why it matters for Mars
A Mars trip would last 2–3 years with no resupply. Closed-loop life support that recycles water and air almost completely is essential.
The same technologies have been adapted for water purification in disaster zones and remote villages on Earth.

cards.title: Paseos espaciales
cards.text: Los paseos espaciales duran de seis a ocho horas. El traje es una mininave con oxígeno, refrigeración y presión. Los astronautas van siempre atados con un cable.

deep.x: A spacewalk, or EVA (extravehicular activity), is one of the riskiest jobs in space. Astronauts install equipment, repair the station and fix science instruments, working in pairs and always tethered.
The suit

A spacesuit is a one-person spacecraft: it provides oxygen, removes CO₂, protects against micrometeoroids and temperature extremes from about −150 °C to +120 °C, and has water-cooled underwear to remove body heat.
Preparing
Suits run at lower pressure than the station, so astronauts first breathe pure oxygen to purge nitrogen from their blood, avoiding the bends, like divers.
Real dangers

x: In 1965 Leonov's suit ballooned; he had to vent air to get back inside
In 2013 Luca Parmitano's helmet filled with water, nearly drowning him
Hands tire quickly working against stiff, pressurised gloves

deep.x: Stiff gloves cause fingernail damage, so astronauts often trim nails very short before spacewalks.

cards.title: El efecto perspectiva

steps: Ver la Tierra desde el espacio

cards.text: Muchos astronautas cuentan que su forma de ver las cosas cambia después de contemplar la Tierra desde el espacio: una frágil bola azul sin fronteras visibles.

deep.x: Author Frank White coined "the overview effect" in 1987 for the shift in perception many astronauts describe: seeing Earth whole, with no visible borders and a paper-thin atmosphere, creates a sense of unity and fragility.
In their words
Astronauts often say the atmosphere looks like a thin blue line, "like the skin of an apple". Many return with stronger feelings about protecting the planet.
Earth seen from orbit

x: Sunrises and sunsets every 45 minutes
Lightning flashing across storm clouds
Auroras below the station
The Sahara's dust blowing over the Atlantic

deep.x: Researchers study whether virtual reality can give people on Earth a taste of the overview effect.

cards.title: Volver a casa
cards.text: Tras meses en órbita, los astronautas necesitan semanas para readaptarse: el equilibrio falla y todo pesa. Algunos olvidan la gravedad y sueltan objetos en el aire.

deep.x: Returning from months in orbit is physically hard. The brain has adapted to weightlessness, so on return gravity feels overwhelming: heads feel heavy, walking is wobbly and turning causes dizziness.
The landing

Soyuz capsules land under parachutes on the steppes of Kazakhstan, firing small rockets a metre above the ground. Crew Dragon splashes down in the ocean. Recovery teams help crews out, often in reclining chairs.
Rehabilitation

x: About 45 days of supervised rehabilitation with physiotherapists
Bone density can take years to recover, and some loss may be permanent
Astronauts report forgetting gravity: letting go of cups, expecting them to float

deep.x: ESA astronaut Tim Peake said that after landing even his tongue felt heavy, making it hard to speak at first.

quiz.q: ¿Por qué los astronautas comen tortillas de trigo en lugar de pan?
options: Las migas flotan y son peligrosas
quiz.explain: Las migas pueden meterse en los equipos.

quiz.q: ¿Por qué los astronautas crecen en el espacio?
options: La columna se estira sin gravedad
quiz.explain: Unos 3 cm, de forma temporal.

lessons.title: Observar el cielo
lessons.summary: Cómo orientarte en el cielo nocturno.

cards.title: Constelaciones

items.l: estrellas visibles en una noche oscura

cards.text: Las constelaciones son figuras de estrellas que nombraron culturas antiguas. Los astrónomos reconocen 88 oficiales. Sus estrellas no suelen estar cerca unas de otras en el espacio.

deep.x: A constellation is a pattern of stars, and since 1922 also an official region of the sky. The International Astronomical Union recognises 88 constellations that together tile the entire sky, so every star belongs to exactly one.
Patterns aren't neighbours
Stars in a constellation usually lie at very different distances. The stars of Orion's belt are about 700–1,300 light-years away, unrelated to each other except by line of sight.
Asterisms
Some famous patterns aren't official constellations. The Big Dipper (or Plough) is part of Ursa Major; the Summer Triangle links stars from three constellations.
Many cultures, many skies
Aboriginal Australians saw an "Emu in the Sky" in dark dust lanes; Chinese astronomers divided the sky into 28 lunar mansions; Polynesian navigators used star paths to cross the Pacific.
Several southern constellations, like Telescopium and Microscopium, were named by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s after scientific instruments.

cards.title: Encontrar la estrella Polar
cards.text: Sigue hacia arriba las dos estrellas del extremo del «cazo» del Carro unas cinco veces la distancia entre ellas y llegarás a la Polar, que apenas se mueve y marca el norte.

deep.x: Polaris lies almost exactly above Earth's North Pole, so as Earth spins, it stays nearly fixed while other stars circle around it. Its altitude above the horizon equals your latitude: about 39° in Lisbon.

steps: Two pointer stars on the bowl

deep.x: Not the brightest
Polaris is only about the 48th brightest star: moderately bright, not dazzling. People often expect it to be brighter.

deep.w: The North Star is the brightest star in the sky
deep.r: It's only moderately bright; Sirius is the brightest

deep.x: Navigation
Sailors, including Portuguese navigators, measured Polaris' height with quadrants and astrolabes to find their latitude. Near the equator, Polaris sinks to the horizon; south of it, it's invisible.
Pole stars change
Earth's axis wobbles in a 26,000-year cycle (precession). About 4,500 years ago the pole star was Thuban; in about 12,000 years it will be Vega.
No equivalent bright star marks the South Pole; southern navigators use the Southern Cross instead.

cards.title: El cielo gira
cards.text: Las estrellas salen por el este y se ponen por el oeste porque la Tierra gira. En las fotos de larga exposición, las estrellas trazan círculos alrededor del polo celeste.

deep.x: As Earth rotates west to east, the whole sky appears to turn east to west around the celestial poles, once every 23 hours 56 minutes. Stars near Polaris never set; they're called circumpolar.
Circumpolar stars
From Portugal, stars within about 39° of Polaris never set, including the Big Dipper and Cassiopeia. Farther south, fewer stars are circumpolar.
Star trails
A long-exposure photo pointed at Polaris shows stars as concentric arcs. A full circle would need a 24-hour exposure in darkness, only possible in polar winter.
Earlier each night
Each night, a star rises about 4 minutes earlier, adding up to 2 hours a month. That's why the constellations shift with the seasons.
The 4-minute difference is why a sidereal day (23 h 56 min) is shorter than a solar day.

cards.title: Estrellas de cada estación
cards.text: Mientras la Tierra gira alrededor del Sol, vemos de noche constelaciones distintas a lo largo del año. Orión reina en las noches de invierno; Escorpio, en las de verano.

deep.x: At night we look away from the Sun. As Earth orbits, the night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations dominate the evening sky through the year.
The zodiac

The Sun appears to move through 13 constellations along the ecliptic over a year, including Ophiuchus, which astrology ignores. The traditional zodiac dates are also off by about a month because of precession.

items.b: 12 signs, fixed dates from ~2,000 years ago
13 constellations on the ecliptic, dates shifted

deep.x: Highlights from Portugal

x: **Winter**: Orion, Sirius, the Pleiades cluster
**Spring**: Leo's sickle, Arcturus
**Summer**: the Milky Way through Sagittarius and Scorpius, low in the south
**Autumn**: the Andromeda galaxy, Pegasus' great square

deep.w: Your zodiac sign is the constellation the Sun was in at your birth
deep.r: Due to precession, the Sun was usually in the previous constellation

cards.title: Orión
cards.text: Orión es fácil de encontrar: tres estrellas brillantes en fila forman su cinturón. La roja Betelgeuse marca un hombro y la azul Rigel, un pie.

deep.x: Orion, the Hunter, is one of the most recognisable constellations, visible from almost anywhere on Earth because it straddles the celestial equator. It dominates winter evenings in the Northern Hemisphere.
The Orion Nebula

Below the belt, Orion's "sword" contains a fuzzy patch: the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery 1,300 light-years away where thousands of stars are forming. It's visible with the naked eye on dark nights and stunning in binoculars.
Betelgeuse

Betelgeuse is a red supergiant so large that, placed where the Sun is, it would extend past the orbit of Mars, maybe Jupiter. In 2019–20 it dimmed dramatically after belching out a dust cloud: the "Great Dimming".
A signpost

x: Follow the belt downwards to Sirius, the brightest star
Follow it upwards to Aldebaran and the Pleiades

deep.x: Orion's belt points almost exactly towards Sirius, so the belt is a pointer to the night sky's brightest star.

cards.title: El brillo de las estrellas
cards.text: Los astrónomos miden el brillo en magnitudes: cuanto menor el número, más brillo. Sirio, la estrella más brillante de la noche, tiene −1,5; las más débiles visibles a simple vista rondan +6.

deep.x: Ancient astronomer Hipparchus ranked stars from 1st magnitude (brightest) to 6th (faintest visible). The modern scale keeps that backwards system and makes it precise: each step of 1 magnitude means about 2.5 times brighter; 5 magnitudes means exactly 100 times.
The scale
Apparent vs absolute

Apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks from Earth; absolute magnitude is how bright it would look from a standard distance of 32.6 light-years. Sirius looks bright mainly because it's close; Rigel looks fainter but is far more luminous.
Hubble can detect objects around magnitude 31, about 10 billion times fainter than the faintest star you can see.

cards.title: Los planetas vagan

steps: Un mes después: se ha movido entre las estrellas

cards.text: «Planeta» viene del griego «errante»: los planetas se mueven respecto a las estrellas de fondo a lo largo de semanas, siempre cerca del camino del Sol, la eclíptica.

deep.x: Ancient sky-watchers noticed five bright "stars" that moved against the fixed constellations: the planets, from the Greek *planētēs*, "wanderer". All stay close to the ecliptic, because the Solar System is flat.

steps: Weeks later: moved along the ecliptic

deep.x: Retrograde motion
Sometimes a planet seems to stop and move backwards for weeks. This happens when Earth, on its faster inside track, overtakes an outer planet, like passing a slower car on a motorway.
Mercury retrograde
Mercury appears to go retrograde about three times a year. Astronomically it's just a viewing angle; it has no effect on phones, emails or relationships.

deep.w: Mercury retrograde causes chaos
deep.r: It's an optical effect of orbital motion with no influence on Earth

deep.x: Conjunctions

When planets appear close together in the sky, it's a conjunction: a lovely sight, though they're actually hundreds of millions of km apart. In December 2020, Jupiter and Saturn appeared closer than at any time since 1623.
Copernicus' explanation of retrograde motion was one of the strongest arguments for a Sun-centred Solar System.

cards.title: La franja de la Vía Láctea

steps: Estamos dentro de un disco plano
Miramos a lo largo del disco

cards.text: En una noche oscura, una franja pálida cruza el cielo: es la luz combinada de miles de millones de estrellas del disco de nuestra galaxia, vista de canto desde dentro.

deep.x: The Milky Way is shaped like a thin disc. From inside, looking along the disc we see a band crowded with stars; looking out of it, we see far fewer. The band's dark lanes are clouds of dust blocking distant starlight.

steps: We sit inside a flat disc
Look along it: band of stars

deep.x: Best seen

x: On moonless nights away from cities, ideally where the sky is rated Bortle 1–3
From Portugal, the brightest part, towards the galactic centre in Sagittarius, is low in the south in summer
The Alentejo and the interior mountains have some of Europe's darkest skies

deep.x: Its name

The Greeks saw spilled milk from the goddess Hera: *galaxias*, from *gala*, milk, gave us "galaxy". In Portuguese it's the Via Láctea, and pilgrims once called it the Way of St James, guiding to Santiago de Compostela.
Galileo was the first to show with a telescope, in 1610, that the Milky Way's glow is made of countless faint stars.

cards.title: Usar bien los ojos

items: Mira un poco de lado los objetos débiles

cards.text: Tus ojos necesitan 20–30 minutos a oscuras para adaptarse del todo. Usa una luz roja para leer mapas, porque el rojo apenas altera la visión nocturna.

deep.x: Your eye adapts to darkness in two stages: pupils widen within seconds, then the retina's rod cells build up a light-sensitive pigment, rhodopsin, over 20–30 minutes. One glance at a bright phone resets much of it.
Tricks of experienced observers

x: **Red light**: rods are almost blind to deep red, so red torches preserve night vision
**Averted vision**: look slightly to the side of a faint object; the edges of the retina have more rods
**Breathing and comfort**: a reclining chair and warm clothes help you stay patient
**Phone apps** with night mode turn the screen red

deep.x: Why stars look colourless
Faint light is seen by rods, which don't sense colour, so most stars look white. Bright stars like Betelgeuse and Rigel show their orange and blue tints.
Use binoculars before a telescope: 7×50 or 10×50 binoculars show craters, moons of Jupiter and star clusters.

cards.title: Tu primera noche
cards.text: Elige una noche sin luna, aléjate de las luces, empieza por la Luna o un planeta brillante y luego busca Orión o el Carro. Unos prismáticos muestran mucho más de lo que esperarías.

deep.x: Good stargazing needs a plan. Check the Moon phase (new Moon is best for faint objects), the weather and cloud forecasts, and a dark location.

items: Bring warm clothes and a red light

deep.x: A beginner's route
What to try with binoculars

x: The Moon's craters, best along the shadow line, not at full Moon
Jupiter's four big moons
The Pleiades star cluster
The Andromeda galaxy, a faint smudge 2.5 million light-years away

deep.x: Events to plan for

x: Meteor showers: Perseids in August, Geminids in December
Eclipses and planetary conjunctions
ISS passes, listed on apps and websites

deep.x: In Portugal, astronomy clubs and Ciência Viva centres hold free public observing nights with telescopes.

quiz.q: ¿Cómo se encuentra la estrella Polar?
options: Con las estrellas guía del Carro
quiz.explain: Marca el norte.

quiz.q: ¿Qué brilla más: magnitud 1 o magnitud 5?
quiz.explain: Cuanto menor el número, más brillo.

lessons.title: Asteroides, cometas e impactos
lessons.summary: Rocas espaciales y cómo defendemos la Tierra.

cards.title: El cinturón de asteroides

items.r: Casi todo vacío: las sondas lo cruzan sin peligro

cards.text: Entre Marte y Júpiter orbitan millones de cuerpos rocosos. Pese a lo que muestran las películas, están muy separados: las naves cruzan el cinturón sin tener que esquivar nada.

deep.x: The main belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, about 2.1 to 3.3 AU from the Sun. It contains more than a million asteroids over 1 km, yet its total mass is only about 3% of the Moon's, and half of that is in four bodies: Ceres, Vesta, Pallas and Hygiea.
Why no planet formed
Jupiter's strong gravity stirred up the region, making collisions too violent for rocks to stick together. Many fragments were flung out, leaving a sparse belt.
Mostly empty space
The average distance between asteroids over 1 km is around a million km. More than a dozen spacecraft have crossed the belt without needing to dodge.

deep.w: The belt is a dense field of rocks
deep.r: Typical gaps are hundreds of thousands to millions of km

deep.x: Families
Collisions shatter larger asteroids into "families" sharing similar orbits. Vesta's family came from a giant impact that also sent meteorites to Earth; we have pieces of Vesta in museums.
Kirkwood gaps, empty zones in the belt, mark orbits where Jupiter's regular tugs clear asteroids out.

cards.title: Ceres
cards.text: Ceres, el mayor objeto del cinturón de asteroides, con unos 940 km de diámetro, está clasificado como planeta enano. La sonda Dawn de la NASA encontró brillantes depósitos de sal en su superficie.

deep.x: Ceres, discovered by Giuseppe Piazzi on 1 January 1801, was first called a planet, then an asteroid, and since 2006 a dwarf planet. It's the only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System and is large enough to be round.
Dawn's discoveries

NASA's Dawn spacecraft, using efficient ion engines, orbited first Vesta and then Ceres. It found bright spots in Occator Crater: deposits of sodium carbonate salts left by briny water seeping up from below.
A wet world

x: Ceres may be about a quarter water ice by mass
It has ammonia-bearing clays, suggesting it formed farther out and migrated inwards
Organic molecules were detected on its surface

deep.x: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different bodies beyond the Earth–Moon system.

cards.title: Anatomía de un cometa
cards.text: Un cometa es una «bola de nieve sucia» de hielo y polvo de unos pocos km. Cerca del Sol, el hielo se convierte en gas y forma una cabeza brillante y colas que siempre apuntan en sentido contrario al Sol.

deep.x: A comet's nucleus is a dark, porous lump of ice, dust and organic material, typically 1–20 km across, darker than charcoal. Far from the Sun it's inert. Within roughly 3 AU, sunlight turns ice directly into gas, which drags dust with it.

items: Ion tail: blue, straight, pushed by solar wind

deep.x: Two tails

The **ion tail** is made of charged gas swept straight back by the solar wind, glowing blue. The **dust tail** is pushed more gently by sunlight pressure and curves along the comet's path. Both point away from the Sun, even when the comet moves outwards.
Rosetta

ESA's Rosetta orbited comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko for two years (2014–16) and dropped the Philae lander on it. The comet was shaped like a rubber duck and smelled, according to its gas, of rotten eggs, ammonia and almonds.

events.l: Rosetta lands on the comet, mission ends

deep.x: Comet tails can stretch over 100 million km, nearly the Earth–Sun distance.

cards.title: El cometa Halley
cards.text: En 1705, Edmond Halley predijo que un cometa visto en 1531, 1607 y 1682 volvería en 1758. Volvió, ya después de su muerte. Su próximo regreso será en 2061.

deep.x: Halley's Comet returns roughly every 76 years. Edmond Halley, using Newton's new laws, realised that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were the same object and predicted its return in late 1758. It reappeared on Christmas night 1758, after Halley's death, a triumph for Newtonian physics.
Halley in history

x: Its 1066 appearance was seen as an omen before the Battle of Hastings and embroidered on the Bayeux Tapestry
Giotto painted it as the Star of Bethlehem around 1305
In 1910 Earth passed through its tail, and some sold "comet pills" to frightened people

deep.x: The 1986 flotilla
Spacecraft from Europe, the USSR and Japan met the comet. ESA's Giotto flew within 600 km of the nucleus and photographed it: a dark, peanut-shaped body 15 km long with jets of gas.
Meteor showers from Halley
Dust shed by Halley produces two meteor showers each year: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October.
Mark Twain was born in 1835 during Halley's appearance and predicted he'd die when it returned; he died in 1910, the day after its perihelion.

cards.title: De dónde vienen los cometas
cards.text: Los cometas de periodo corto vienen del cinturón de Kuiper, más allá de Neptuno; los de periodo largo, de la lejana nube de Oort, una capa que quizá esté a un año luz.

deep.x: Comets are frozen leftovers from the outer Solar System. They're stored in two great reservoirs and occasionally nudged inwards.
The Oort Cloud

Proposed by Jan Oort in 1950, the Oort Cloud may contain trillions of icy bodies, extending perhaps a light-year or more. It has never been seen directly; its existence is inferred from comets arriving from all directions with very long orbits.
How comets get nudged
Interstellar visitors
Some comets come from other stars entirely. 'Oumuamua (2017), 2I/Borisov (2019) and 3I/ATLAS (2025) passed through our Solar System on one-time paths, carrying material from other planetary systems.
Long-period comets can appear with little warning; Hale–Bopp in 1997 was visible to the naked eye for 18 months.

cards.title: El asesino de los dinosaurios
cards.text: Hace unos 66 millones de años, un asteroide de unos 10 km cayó en el Yucatán (México) y formó el cráter de Chicxulub. El polvo y los incendios cambiaron el clima y acabaron con los dinosaurios no avianos.

deep.x: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid about 10 km wide struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula at around 20 km/s. The Chicxulub crater it left is about 180 km wide, now buried under sediment.
The evidence

In 1980 Luis and Walter Alvarez found a thin clay layer worldwide, rich in iridium, an element rare on Earth's surface but common in asteroids, exactly at the boundary between the Cretaceous and the Paleogene. The crater itself was identified in 1991.
Winners and losers

x: All non-bird dinosaurs, pterosaurs and most marine reptiles disappeared
Small mammals, birds, crocodiles and turtles survived
Mammals then diversified, eventually including us

deep.x: Volcanoes too?
India's Deccan Traps erupted vast lava floods around the same time, adding climate stress. Most scientists now see the impact as the main trigger.
The asteroid hit sulphur-rich rock; if it had struck deep ocean, the climate effects and extinction might have been much smaller.

cards.title: Tunguska
cards.text: En 1908, un objeto explotó sobre Siberia y derribó unos 80 millones de árboles en 2000 km². No murió nadie porque la zona era muy remota.

deep.x: On 30 June 1908, a fireball exploded over the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia, about 5–10 km above the ground. It was probably a stony asteroid or comet fragment roughly 50–60 m wide.
No crater
Because it exploded in the air, there was no crater. Trees at the centre were stripped but left standing, while those further out were flattened radially, pointing away from the blast.
Late investigation
The remote area wasn't studied until Leonid Kulik's expedition in 1927. Eyewitnesses 60 km away described being thrown from their chairs and feeling intense heat.
If it hit a city
An air burst of that size over a big city would cause enormous destruction. That's part of why 30 June is now Asteroid Day, to raise awareness of impact risks.
For several nights after the event, skies over Europe were so bright that people could read newspapers outdoors at midnight.

cards.title: Cheliábinsk
cards.text: En 2013, una roca de 20 metros explotó sobre Cheliábinsk (Rusia). La onda expansiva rompió ventanas e hirió a unas 1500 personas, sobre todo por los cristales.

deep.x: On 15 February 2013, a 20 m, 12,000-tonne asteroid entered over Russia at about 19 km/s. It exploded about 30 km up with the energy of roughly 500 kilotons of TNT, about 30 Hiroshima bombs.
Why people were hurt
The flash was brighter than the Sun. Curious residents went to windows to look, and about a minute later the shock wave arrived, shattering glass. Most injuries came from flying glass.
Unseen until it hit
It came from the direction of the Sun, where telescopes can't look, so nobody saw it coming. By coincidence, a different, unrelated asteroid passed close to Earth the same day.
Lessons

x: Even small asteroids can cause damage
Dashcams in Russia captured the event, giving scientists precise trajectories
It boosted funding for telescopes to find smaller asteroids

deep.x: A 650 kg fragment was recovered from Lake Chebarkul and is displayed in a local museum.

cards.title: Defensa planetaria
cards.text: Los telescopios siguen los asteroides cercanos a la Tierra. En 2022, la nave DART de la NASA chocó contra la pequeña luna Dimorfo y cambió su órbita: la primera prueba de desvío de un asteroide.

deep.x: Planetary defence is about finding dangerous asteroids early and, if necessary, changing their path. Survey telescopes have found over 95% of near-Earth asteroids larger than 1 km; the hunt continues for smaller ones.
DART

On 26 September 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, a 160 m moonlet orbiting the asteroid Didymos, at 6.1 km/s. It shortened Dimorphos' orbit by 33 minutes, far more than the minimum goal of 73 seconds, partly because ejected debris acted like a rocket.
Hera
ESA's Hera mission, launched in 2024, will reach Didymos in 2026 to study the crater and measure Dimorphos' mass, turning DART into a repeatable technique.
Other options

x: Kinetic impactor: hit it hard, like DART
Gravity tractor: hover nearby for years, gently pulling it off course
Nuclear device: last resort for large, late-detected threats

deep.x: The key is time: a tiny nudge decades in advance is far easier than a big push weeks before impact.

cards.title: ¿Cuánto deberíamos preocuparnos?
cards.text: Cada día caen rocas pequeñas que arden en la atmósfera. Los impactos grandes son raros: los capaces de destruir una ciudad, cada pocos siglos; los que acabaron con los dinosaurios, cada ~100 millones de años.

deep.x: Impact risk is low probability but high consequence. The smaller the object, the more often it arrives, and the less harm it does.

items.b: every couple of weeks, burns up

deep.x: Known threats

No known asteroid has a significant chance of hitting Earth in the next century. Apophis, 340 m, will pass safely at about 32,000 km on 13 April 2029, closer than geostationary satellites and visible to the naked eye from Europe.
The Torino scale

Astronomers rate impact threats from 0 (no hazard) to 10 (certain global catastrophe). Almost all objects sit at 0. When an asteroid briefly scores higher, extra observations nearly always bring it back to 0.
In perspective
Your lifetime risk of dying in an impact is extremely small but not zero, comparable to some rare natural hazards. Unlike earthquakes, though, impacts are preventable with enough warning.
NASA's NEO Surveyor telescope, planned for launch around 2027, is designed to find most near-Earth asteroids larger than 140 m.

quiz.q: ¿Hacia dónde apuntan las colas de un cometa?
quiz.explain: Las empujan la luz y el viento solar.

quiz.q: ¿Qué demostró la misión DART de la NASA?
options: Que una nave puede cambiar la órbita de un asteroide
quiz.explain: Al chocar contra Dimorfo en 2022.

quiz.q: ¿Dónde está Ceres?
quiz.explain: Es un planeta enano.

lessons.title: Materia oscura y energía oscura
lessons.summary: El 95 % del universo que no podemos ver.

cards.title: De qué está hecho el universo
cards.text: La materia ordinaria, todo lo que está hecho de átomos, es solo un 5 % del universo. El resto es materia oscura y energía oscura, que no podemos ver directamente.

deep.x: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background, galaxy clusters and supernovae all agree on the universe's recipe: about 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter and 68% dark energy.
Even ordinary matter is mostly hidden
Of the 5% that's ordinary matter, only a small part is in stars. Most is hot, thin gas between galaxies, hard to detect.
How we know

x: The pattern of hot and cold spots in the cosmic microwave background depends on these amounts
Galaxy rotation and cluster motions show extra unseen mass
Distant supernovae reveal accelerating expansion

deep.x: Everything humans have ever seen through any telescope makes up about 5% of what's out there.

cards.title: Giran demasiado rápido
cards.text: En los años 70, Vera Rubin descubrió que las estrellas del borde de las galaxias orbitan tan rápido como las del centro. La materia visible por sí sola no podría retenerlas: algo invisible añade gravedad.

deep.x: In a solar system, outer planets move slower than inner ones because most mass is at the centre. Astronomers expected the same for stars in galaxies. In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured galaxy rotation and found outer stars moving just as fast as inner ones: "flat rotation curves".
The interpretation
Flat rotation curves mean galaxies must contain much more mass than we see, spread in a large halo extending far beyond the visible disc. Without it, the outer stars would fly off.

items: Dark matter halo: most of the mass

deep.x: Vera Rubin's legacy

Rubin faced barriers as a woman in astronomy, yet her work became the cornerstone evidence for dark matter. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which released its first images in 2025, bears her name.
In the Milky Way, dark matter may outweigh stars and gas by about 5 to 1, perhaps more including the full halo.

cards.title: Fritz Zwicky
cards.text: Ya en 1933, Fritz Zwicky observó que las galaxias del cúmulo de Coma se movían demasiado rápido para que la materia visible las mantuviera unidas. Llamó a la masa que faltaba «dunkle Materie», materia oscura.

deep.x: Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky, working at Caltech, studied the Coma Cluster in 1933. Galaxies were moving so fast that the cluster should have flown apart, unless it contained hundreds of times more mass than its visible light suggested. He called it "dunkle Materie".

steps: Far more than the visible stars

deep.x: Ignored for decades
His conclusion was largely overlooked for 40 years, partly because his estimates were rough and partly because he was famously abrasive. Rubin's rotation curves in the 1970s brought the idea back.
A prolific mind
Zwicky also coined "supernova" with Walter Baade and proposed that supernovae create neutron stars, years before neutron stars were found.
Good ideas can wait decades for evidence and attention to catch up.

cards.title: El cúmulo Bala

steps: El gas se frena y brilla

cards.text: Cuando dos cúmulos de galaxias chocaron, el gas caliente se frenó, pero la mayor parte de la masa, cartografiada por lentes gravitacionales, siguió de largo: una prueba sólida de la materia oscura.

deep.x: The Bullet Cluster is two galaxy clusters that collided about 150 million years ago, 3.7 billion light-years away. It offered one of the most direct pieces of evidence that dark matter is a real substance, not just a quirk of gravity.

steps: Gas clouds smash and slow down
Galaxies and dark matter pass through
Mass and gas end up separated

deep.x: Two maps compared
X-ray telescopes (Chandra) mapped the hot gas, which holds most of the ordinary matter. Gravitational lensing mapped where the mass actually is. The mass sat with the galaxies, not with the gas.
Why it matters
Alternative theories that modify gravity struggle to explain mass located away from most ordinary matter. Dark matter that barely interacts, passing through like ghosts, explains it naturally.
The "bullet" is a shock wave of hot gas shaped like a bullet, moving at about 4,500 km/s.

cards.title: ¿Qué podría ser?
cards.text: La materia oscura no emite ni absorbe luz y apenas interactúa. Entre los candidatos hay partículas desconocidas como los WIMP o los axiones. Los detectores bajo tierra no han encontrado nada por ahora.

deep.x: Dark matter must have mass and gravity but almost no interaction with light or ordinary matter. It can't be ordinary atoms, which would show up in measurements of the early universe, so physicists look for new particles.
How we hunt

x: **Direct detection**: huge tanks of liquid xenon deep underground wait for a dark matter particle to bump a nucleus
**Indirect detection**: telescopes look for radiation from dark matter particles annihilating
**Colliders**: the LHC tries to create dark matter particles

deep.x: Modified gravity
A minority of physicists propose that gravity behaves differently at very low accelerations (MOND). It explains galaxy rotation well but struggles with clusters and the cosmic microwave background.
Billions of dark matter particles may be passing through your body every second without leaving any trace.

cards.title: Energía oscura
cards.text: En 1998, dos equipos descubrieron que la expansión del universo se está acelerando, no frenando. Algo, llamado energía oscura, separa el espacio. Ganó el Premio Nobel de 2011.

deep.x: In 1998 two teams measuring distant Type Ia supernovae found they were fainter, so farther, than expected. The universe's expansion is accelerating. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess won the 2011 Nobel Prize.
What might it be?
The simplest explanation is Einstein's "cosmological constant": an energy belonging to empty space itself. As space expands, there's more of it, so its push grows relative to matter's pull.
A cosmic tug-of-war
For the first ~9 billion years, gravity slowed the expansion. About 5 billion years ago, dark energy took over and expansion started to accelerate.
Is it changing?
Recent results from the DESI survey (2024–25) hint that dark energy might be weakening over time. If confirmed, it would change our picture of the universe's future.
Einstein called his cosmological constant his "biggest blunder"; it may turn out to be one of his best ideas.

cards.title: Candelas estándar
cards.text: Todas las supernovas de tipo Ia alcanzan más o menos el mismo brillo máximo, así que lo brillantes que parecen nos dice a qué distancia están, como calcular la distancia de una bombilla conocida.

deep.x: To measure distance, astronomers need objects whose true brightness they know: "standard candles". Comparing true and apparent brightness gives distance, just as you can judge how far away a 100 W bulb is from how dim it looks.
The cosmic distance ladder

items: Type Ia supernovae: billions of ly

deep.x: Type Ia supernovae

They happen when a white dwarf in a binary system gains matter until it reaches about 1.4 Suns and explodes. Because they explode at a similar mass, their peak brightness is similar, and so bright they're visible across billions of light-years.
The Hubble tension
Measuring the expansion rate with the distance ladder gives about 73 km/s per megaparsec; measuring it from the early universe gives about 67. This "Hubble tension" may signal new physics.
Henrietta Leavitt's 1912 discovery of the Cepheid period–luminosity rule made the first rungs of the ladder possible.

cards.title: La red cósmica
cards.text: A la mayor escala, las galaxias forman una red de filamentos y paredes alrededor de enormes vacíos, modelada por la gravedad de la materia oscura.

deep.x: Maps of millions of galaxies reveal a vast web: galaxies gather along filaments and sheets, with clusters at the knots, surrounding enormous voids up to hundreds of millions of light-years across.
How it formed

Tiny density ripples in the early universe, visible in the cosmic microwave background, grew under gravity. Dark matter collapsed first into a scaffolding; ordinary gas flowed along it and formed galaxies at the densest points.

steps: Tiny ripples after the Big Bang

deep.x: Simulations
Supercomputer simulations like Millennium and IllustrisTNG start from early-universe conditions, add dark matter and physics, and reproduce a web that looks strikingly like the real one.
Our place
The Milky Way sits in a modest filament near the edge of the Local Void. Galaxy surveys have mapped the Laniakea Supercluster, our "immeasurable heaven", about 500 million light-years across.
The cosmic web's structure looks remarkably similar to networks of neurons in the brain, though the similarity is only visual.

cards.title: Euclid
cards.text: El telescopio Euclid de la ESA, lanzado en 2023, está cartografiando miles de millones de galaxias para medir cómo la materia oscura y la energía oscura han dado forma al universo.

deep.x: ESA's Euclid space telescope, launched on 1 July 2023, sits at the L2 point and is mapping a third of the sky. Its goal: a 3D map of billions of galaxies over 10 billion years of cosmic history to understand dark matter and dark energy.
Two techniques

x: **Weak lensing**: measures tiny distortions in galaxy shapes, revealing the dark matter between us and them
**Galaxy clustering**: measures how galaxies are spaced at different eras, tracking expansion

deep.x: A wide view
Euclid's field of view is about 2.5 times the area of the full Moon, much wider than Hubble or Webb, letting it survey huge areas efficiently.
Portuguese astronomers contribute to the Euclid Consortium, including science teams at the Institute of Astrophysics and Space Sciences in Lisbon and Porto.

cards.title: Ciencia en la frontera
cards.text: Materia oscura y energía oscura son nombres para cosas que podemos medir pero que aún no entendemos. Lo desconocido es donde ocurre la ciencia más emocionante.

deep.x: Dark matter and dark energy are placeholders: names for effects we can measure precisely without knowing their cause. That's normal in science. Neptune began as "something pulling Uranus"; Mercury's odd orbit led to relativity.
Possible futures
The open questions

x: What is dark matter made of?
Is dark energy constant, or does it evolve?
Why is the Hubble constant measured differently by different methods?
Are these signs of a deeper theory linking gravity and quantum physics?

deep.x: Admitting what we don't know is the start of discovery; the 95% we don't understand is where the next revolutions may come from.

quiz.q: ¿Qué parte del universo es materia ordinaria?
quiz.explain: El resto es materia oscura y energía oscura.

quiz.q: ¿Con qué está relacionada la energía oscura?
options: Con la expansión acelerada del universo
quiz.explain: Se descubrió en 1998.

lessons.title: Satélites y GPS
lessons.summary: Las máquinas invisibles que tenemos encima.

cards.title: ¿Cuántos hay?
cards.text: Más de 10 000 satélites activos orbitan la Tierra; la mayoría se han lanzado en los últimos años para constelaciones de internet. El primero, el Sputnik, se lanzó en 1957.

deep.x: Satellite numbers stayed in the low thousands for decades, then exploded after 2019 as companies launched internet "megaconstellations". Starlink alone accounts for well over half of all active satellites.
Who owns them?
Why the boom?

x: Reusable rockets cut launch costs dramatically
Satellites shrank: "CubeSats" can be the size of a shoebox
Many small satellites in low orbit give fast internet with low delay

deep.x: Sputnik's legacy

Sputnik 1 transmitted beeps for 21 days and burned up after three months. Tracking its signal, American scientists realised they could find their own position from a satellite's known orbit, the seed of GPS.
Thousands more satellites are planned; estimates suggest tens of thousands could be in orbit by the 2030s.

cards.title: Tipos de órbita
cards.text: Los satélites ocupan órbitas distintas según su función: órbita baja para imágenes e internet, media para navegación y geoestacionaria para televisión y meteorología.

deep.x: Different jobs need different heights. Lower orbits give sharper images and faster signals; higher orbits see more of the Earth at once and need fewer satellites.
The main families

items.b: passes overhead at the same local time daily

deep.x: Sun-synchronous orbits
These polar orbits are tilted so the satellite crosses each place at the same local solar time every day, giving consistent lighting for comparing images over months and years.
Highly elliptical orbits
Molniya orbits, used by Russia, swing high over the far north for hours, serving regions that geostationary satellites see poorly.
Low-orbit satellites eventually fall back and burn up because of thin air drag; geostationary ones would stay for millions of years.

cards.title: Cómo funciona el GPS
cards.text: Tu móvil recibe señales horarias de al menos cuatro satélites. A partir de las diminutas diferencias en el tiempo de llegada, calcula su posición con un margen de pocos metros.

deep.x: Each GPS satellite broadcasts its precise position and the exact time from an onboard atomic clock. Your receiver notes when each signal arrives; the delay, multiplied by the speed of light, gives the distance to each satellite.

v.f: distance = signal delay × speed of light

deep.x: Trilateration
Knowing your distance from one satellite puts you somewhere on a sphere. Two spheres intersect in a circle; three narrow it to two points, one of which is usually far out in space.
Accuracy

x: Phones typically get 3–5 m; combining satellite systems and Wi-Fi improves it
Dual-frequency receivers in newer phones correct atmospheric errors
Surveyors using correction stations reach centimetre accuracy

deep.x: Selective availability
Until May 2000 the US deliberately degraded civilian GPS to about 100 m accuracy. Switching it off overnight made car navigation practical.
Your phone doesn't send anything to the satellites: GPS reception is one-way, which is why it works offline.

cards.title: ¿Por qué cuatro satélites?
cards.text: Tres satélites fijan tu posición en 3D; un cuarto corrige el reloj barato e impreciso de tu móvil. Más satélites mejoran la precisión.

deep.x: To calculate position from timing, you need perfectly synchronised clocks. Satellites have atomic clocks; your phone has a cheap quartz clock that drifts. That unknown clock error is a fourth unknown, alongside latitude, longitude and altitude.
Four equations, four unknowns

With signals from four satellites, the receiver solves four equations at once, correcting its own clock to nanosecond accuracy as a bonus. Your phone is, in effect, briefly synchronised to an atomic clock.
More is better

x: Modern receivers often track 20–40 satellites from several systems
Satellites spread across the sky give better geometry than clustered ones
In cities, tall buildings block and reflect signals, causing errors ("urban canyons")

deep.x: GPS timing synchronises mobile phone networks and power grids worldwide, a use as important as navigation.

cards.title: Galileo
cards.text: El sistema de navegación propio de Europa, Galileo, tiene más de 25 satélites. Los móviles combinan GPS (EE. UU.), Galileo (UE), GLONASS (Rusia) y BeiDou (China).

deep.x: Galileo is the European Union's global satellite navigation system, run with ESA. Europe built it to have its own civilian-controlled system, independent of the US military's GPS.
Features

x: Over 25 satellites in medium orbit, about 23,000 km up
Free open service accurate to about a metre with modern phones
High-accuracy service with centimetre-level precision
Search-and-rescue: detects distress beacons and confirms to the sender that help is coming

deep.x: A troubled start
Two satellites launched in 2014 ended up in the wrong, elliptical orbits because of a rocket fault. They were later repurposed to test Einstein's general relativity with record precision.
Better together
Modern phones use all four systems at once. More satellites in view means faster, more reliable fixes, especially in cities.
Each Galileo satellite is named after a child who won a European drawing competition.

cards.title: Satélites meteorológicos
cards.text: Los satélites geoestacionarios fotografían la misma mitad de la Tierra cada pocos minutos, mientras que los de órbita polar recorren todo el planeta dos veces al día. Las previsiones dependen de ambos.

deep.x: Modern forecasting relies on satellites for most of its input. They measure clouds, temperatures at different heights, humidity, winds (by tracking cloud motion) and sea-surface temperatures.
Meteosat
EUMETSAT's Meteosat satellites have watched Europe and Africa since 1977. The newest generation, Meteosat Third Generation, adds a lightning imager that maps flashes day and night.
What they see

x: **Visible**: clouds by day
**Infrared**: cloud-top temperatures, day and night; colder tops mean taller storms
**Water vapour**: moisture in the upper atmosphere, revealing jet streams

deep.x: Hurricane forecasts have improved so much that 3-day track errors today are smaller than 1-day errors in the 1970s.

cards.title: Observación de la Tierra
cards.text: Los satélites Sentinel del programa europeo Copernicus vigilan gratis incendios, inundaciones, cultivos, el nivel del mar y el hielo. Bomberos y agricultores portugueses usan sus datos.

deep.x: Copernicus is the EU's Earth observation programme, run with ESA. Its Sentinel satellites provide free, open data used by governments, researchers, farmers and firefighters worldwide.

items.b: radar, sees through clouds and at night

deep.x: In Portugal

x: Mapping burnt areas after wildfires and monitoring recovery
Checking crop health and irrigation needs in the Alentejo
Tracking coastal erosion and dune movement
Watching water levels in reservoirs during droughts

deep.x: Radar sees through clouds
Sentinel-1's radar measures ground movement down to millimetres, revealing subsidence, landslides and how volcanoes swell before eruptions, like on La Palma in 2021.
Sentinel-2 images the whole of Europe's land every 5 days at 10 m resolution, enough to see individual fields.

cards.title: Basura espacial
cards.text: Más de un millón de fragmentos de basura de más de 1 cm orbitan la Tierra a la velocidad de una bala. Una colisión puede crear miles de fragmentos más.

deep.x: Debris includes dead satellites, spent rocket stages and fragments from explosions and collisions. In low orbit it travels at about 7–8 km/s, so even a 1 cm fragment hits with the energy of a hand grenade.
The Kessler syndrome
In 1978 NASA scientist Donald Kessler warned that collisions could produce debris that causes more collisions, a cascade that could make some orbits unusable.
Major events
Solutions

x: Design satellites to de-orbit within a few years after their mission
Avoidance manoeuvres: the ISS dodges debris several times a year
Active removal: ESA's ClearSpace-1 aims to capture and remove debris
International rules against weapons tests that create debris

deep.x: Portugal and the EU contribute to the EU Space Surveillance and Tracking network, which monitors debris and warns operators.

cards.title: Internet por satélite
cards.text: Constelaciones de miles de satélites en órbita baja dan internet rápido en cualquier lugar, incluidos barcos, aviones y pueblos remotos. A los astrónomos les preocupan los trazos que dejan en sus imágenes.

deep.x: Old satellite internet used a few geostationary satellites: wide coverage but slow, with a round-trip delay over half a second. New constellations use thousands of satellites in low orbit, only about 550 km up, giving fibre-like delays of 25–50 ms.
How it works

A dish on the ground tracks satellites electronically as they pass overhead in minutes, switching seamlessly to the next. Newer satellites relay data between each other with lasers, reducing the need for ground stations.
Benefits

x: Internet for ships, planes, remote farms and islands
Backup during disasters when ground networks fail
Connectivity in conflict zones

deep.x: Concerns

x: Streaks in astronomical images and radio interference
Thousands of satellites increasing collision risk
Dependence on a few private companies

deep.x: The EU is planning its own secure constellation, IRIS², to reduce dependence on foreign providers.

cards.title: Portugal en el espacio
cards.text: Portugal entró en la ESA en 2000, fundó la agencia Portugal Space en 2019 y lanzó su primer satélite, el microsatélite PoSAT-1, ya en 1993.

deep.x: Portugal's space sector is small but growing fast. Its first satellite, PoSAT-1, launched in 1993, was a microsatellite of about 50 kg built with the University of Surrey.
Strengths

x: Engineering firms supplying parts for ESA missions, from software to structures
Earth observation for oceans, forests and agriculture
The Azores, in the middle of the Atlantic, are ideal for satellite tracking stations and a planned spaceport on Santa Maria

deep.x: The Atlantic advantage

Ships, cables and weather systems cross the Atlantic, and Portugal's large sea area makes ocean monitoring from space especially valuable. The Atlantic International Research Centre (AIR Centre) is based in the Azores.
Aeros MH-1, launched in 2024, was described as the first satellite designed and built largely in Portugal since PoSAT-1.

quiz.explain: El cuarto corrige el error del reloj.

lessons.title: Los grandes pioneros de la astronomía
lessons.summary: Cómo descubrimos nuestro lugar en el cosmos.

cards.title: Astrónomos de la Antigüedad
cards.text: Los babilonios registraron eclipses durante siglos; los griegos midieron la Tierra. Hacia el 240 a. C., Eratóstenes estimó la circunferencia terrestre usando las sombras de dos ciudades.

deep.x: Ancient peoples watched the sky for calendars, agriculture, navigation and religion. Babylonian scribes kept astronomical diaries for centuries and could predict lunar eclipses using cycles such as the 18-year Saros.
Eratosthenes measures the Earth

At noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down a well in Syene (Aswan). In Alexandria, 800 km north, a stick cast a shadow at about 7°, one-fiftieth of a circle. So Earth's circumference was about 50 × 800 km = 40,000 km, remarkably close to the true 40,075 km.
Other Greek achievements

x: Aristarchus proposed a Sun-centred system around 270 BCE
Hipparchus discovered the precession of the equinoxes and catalogued about 850 stars
The Antikythera mechanism, a geared bronze calculator, predicted eclipses and planet positions

deep.x: Columbus underestimated Earth's size; scholars who used Eratosthenes-style estimates were closer to the truth.

cards.title: El modelo de Ptolomeo
cards.text: El modelo de Ptolomeo, con la Tierra en el centro y los planetas moviéndose en círculos sobre círculos, predecía las posiciones lo bastante bien como para usarse durante 1400 años.

deep.x: Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria around 150 CE, wrote the *Almagest*, which put Earth at the centre with the Sun, Moon and planets moving on circles. To explain retrograde loops, planets moved on small circles (epicycles) riding on bigger ones (deferents).
Why it lasted

Ptolemy's model predicted planetary positions well enough for navigation, calendars and astrology for 1,400 years. It was translated into Arabic and refined by astronomers in Baghdad, Damascus and Samarkand before returning to Europe.
Its weaknesses

x: Many arbitrary adjustments, like off-centre points called equants
No physical explanation for why planets moved that way
Couldn't explain why Mercury and Venus always stay near the Sun without special tweaks

deep.x: A model can make good predictions and still be wrong about how the world really is.

cards.title: Copérnico
cards.text: En 1543, Nicolás Copérnico publicó su modelo con el Sol en el centro, que sacaba a la Tierra del centro del universo. Hizo falta un siglo para que se aceptara ampliamente.

deep.x: Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish canon and astronomer, placed the Sun near the centre with Earth as one of the planets, orbiting yearly and spinning daily. His book *On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres* appeared in 1543, the year he died.

items: planets in order from the Sun

deep.x: What it explained elegantly

x: Retrograde motion: Earth overtaking outer planets
Why Mercury and Venus stay near the Sun: their orbits are inside ours
The order and relative distances of the planets

deep.x: What it didn't fix
Copernicus kept perfect circles, so he still needed epicycles, and his model was not much more accurate than Ptolemy's. It took Kepler's ellipses to make the Sun-centred system clearly superior.
A slow revolution
For decades, many astronomers used Copernicus' tables for calculation without believing Earth moved. Galileo's observations and Kepler's laws gradually made the case.
The phrase "Copernican revolution" now means any change that removes humans from a special central place.

cards.title: Tycho y Kepler
cards.text: Tycho Brahe hizo las mediciones a simple vista más precisas de la historia. Su ayudante, Johannes Kepler, las usó para descubrir que los planetas se mueven en elipses.

deep.x: Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) built the best observatory of his age on the island of Hven, measuring planetary positions to about 1 arcminute without a telescope. He proposed his own hybrid model: the Sun orbits Earth, while the planets orbit the Sun.
Kepler's struggle with Mars
Kepler spent years trying to fit Mars' orbit with circles. The best circle missed Tycho's data by 8 arcminutes. Trusting the data, he abandoned circles and found an ellipse fitted perfectly.
Lessons

x: Precise data can overturn centuries of assumption
Kepler's laws were empirical: they described motion without explaining why
Newton later showed gravity produces exactly Kepler's ellipses

deep.x: Tycho lost part of his nose in a duel over a mathematical dispute and wore a metal replacement.

cards.title: El juicio de Galileo
cards.text: El apoyo de Galileo a un sistema con el Sol en el centro lo llevó a ser juzgado por la Inquisición en 1633. Pasó sus últimos años en arresto domiciliario.

deep.x: In 1616 the Catholic Church declared the Sun-centred idea "formally heretical" and warned Galileo not to hold or defend it. In 1632 he published *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems*, which seemed to mock the Earth-centred view.
The trial

Aged 69, Galileo was tried by the Roman Inquisition, forced to recant and sentenced to house arrest for life. He continued working, writing his important book on motion and materials, *Two New Sciences* (1638).
The legend
The famous line "Eppur si muove" ("and yet it moves"), supposedly muttered after recanting, probably wasn't said at the trial; it first appears in print over a century later.

deep.w: Galileo said "and yet it moves" at his trial
deep.r: The quote first appears over a century later and is probably legend

deep.x: Rehabilitation
In 1992 Pope John Paul II formally acknowledged errors in the Church's handling of the case. The episode remains a powerful symbol of conflicts between authority and evidence.
Galileo's lasting legacy is the method: test ideas against observation and experiment.

cards.title: Newton

steps: Una ley para manzanas y planetas

cards.text: En 1687, los *Principia* de Newton explicaron las leyes de Kepler con la gravitación universal y las leyes del movimiento: la misma física en la Tierra y en el cielo.

deep.x: Isaac Newton's *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* (1687) set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. With them, he derived Kepler's laws, explained tides and predicted the shape of the Earth.
One physics for everything

Before Newton, many believed the heavens obeyed different rules from Earth. Newton showed the same gravity governs a falling apple and the Moon's orbit: a unification that shaped all of later science.
Other achievements

x: Invented calculus, independently of Leibniz
Showed white light is a mixture of colours using prisms
Built the first practical reflecting telescope

deep.x: Halley's role
Edmond Halley encouraged Newton to write the *Principia* and paid for its printing himself when the Royal Society had spent its budget on a book about fish.
Newton spent much of his later life as Warden and Master of the Royal Mint, prosecuting counterfeiters.

cards.title: Herschel
cards.text: William Herschel descubrió Urano en 1781, el primer planeta hallado con telescopio. Su hermana Caroline Herschel descubrió varios cometas.

deep.x: William Herschel, a German-born musician in England, built his own excellent reflecting telescopes. On 13 March 1781 he noticed a "star" that showed a disc and moved: Uranus, doubling the known size of the Solar System.
Mapping the galaxy
Herschel counted stars in hundreds of directions to estimate the Milky Way's shape: the first attempt at mapping our galaxy, concluding it was a flattened disc.
Caroline Herschel

Caroline worked alongside William, discovered eight comets and several nebulae, and became the first woman paid for scientific work in Britain and the first to receive the Royal Astronomical Society's Gold Medal.

items.b: 8 comets, nebula catalogues, first paid female scientist in Britain

deep.x: Discovering infrared
In 1800 William put thermometers in the colours of a sunlight spectrum and found it hottest beyond the red, where no light was visible: infrared radiation.
Herschel was also a prolific composer, writing 24 symphonies before astronomy took over his life.

cards.title: Henrietta Leavitt
cards.text: En 1912, Henrietta Leavitt descubrió que el periodo de ciertas estrellas pulsantes revela su brillo real, lo que dio a los astrónomos una cinta métrica cósmica.

deep.x: Henrietta Swan Leavitt worked as a "computer" at Harvard College Observatory, analysing photographic plates for 30 cents an hour. Studying thousands of variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds, she noticed that brighter Cepheid stars pulsed more slowly.
Why it mattered

Because all the stars in a Magellanic Cloud are about the same distance away, the pattern meant that a Cepheid's period reveals its true luminosity. Find a Cepheid anywhere, time its pulses, and you can calculate its distance.
The Harvard computers
Dozens of women, including Annie Jump Cannon and Williamina Fleming, catalogued and classified hundreds of thousands of stars. Cannon devised the OBAFGKM star classes still used today.
Leavitt died in 1921; a Swedish mathematician wanted to nominate her for a Nobel Prize in 1925, not knowing she'd already died.

cards.title: Hubble y las galaxias

items: la Vía Láctea es el universo
una galaxia entre miles de millones

cards.text: En 1924, Edwin Hubble usó el método de Leavitt para demostrar que Andrómeda está muy lejos de la Vía Láctea. De pronto, el universo contenía innumerables galaxias.

deep.x: In the early 1920s, astronomers debated whether "spiral nebulae" were clouds inside the Milky Way or separate "island universes". In 1923–24, Edwin Hubble found Cepheid stars in the Andromeda nebula using the 2.5 m Hooker telescope, showing it lay far beyond our galaxy.
The expanding universe
Hubble then compared galaxy distances with their redshifts, measured largely by Vesto Slipher and Milton Humason, and found that farther galaxies recede faster: the universe is expanding.
Lemaître's credit
Belgian physicist Georges Lemaître published the expansion law in 1927, two years before Hubble. Since 2018 astronomers officially call it the Hubble–Lemaître law.
The Hubble Space Telescope, launched 1990, was named in his honour; it measured the expansion rate to within a few per cent.

cards.title: Pedro Nunes
cards.text: El matemático portugués Pedro Nunes (1502–1578) mejoró la navegación: estudió las loxodromias e inventó el nonio, una escala para leer ángulos con precisión. Un cráter lunar lleva su nombre.

deep.x: Pedro Nunes (1502–1578), royal cosmographer of Portugal and professor at Coimbra, was one of the great mathematicians of the age of discoveries. He applied mathematics to the practical problems of ocean navigation.
The rhumb line

Nunes showed that a ship holding a constant compass bearing doesn't follow a great circle but spirals towards the pole: the loxodrome, or rhumb line. This insight later shaped the Mercator projection.
The nonius
To read angles more precisely on instruments like astrolabes, Nunes devised a set of concentric scales: the nonius. It inspired the vernier scale used on callipers today.
Legacy

x: A lunar crater, Nonius, is named after him
A Portuguese research centre and schools carry his name
He tutored future kings and navigators

deep.x: Nunes is a reminder that Portugal's voyages were also scientific achievements built on mathematics.

quiz.explain: Con las sombras del mediodía.

lessons.title: El futuro del espacio
lessons.summary: Hacia dónde vamos ahora.

cards.title: Volver a la Luna

steps: Artemis II: tripulación alrededor de la Luna

cards.text: El programa Artemis de la NASA quiere llevar de nuevo seres humanos a la Luna por primera vez desde 1972 y establecer una presencia duradera cerca del polo sur.

deep.x: NASA's Artemis programme aims to land astronauts near the Moon's south pole and build up a sustained presence with international and commercial partners. ESA builds the European Service Module that powers the Orion capsule.

steps: Crew transfers to a lunar lander

deep.x: The missions

events.l: crew of four around the Moon

deep.x: Partners
China's plans

China aims to land astronauts on the Moon around 2030 and, with partners, build an International Lunar Research Station. Its robotic Chang'e missions have already returned samples from both near and far sides.
Artemis II's crew includes Canadian Jeremy Hansen, the first non-American assigned to fly around the Moon.

cards.title: ¿Por qué el polo sur lunar?
cards.text: Sus cráteres en sombra permanente contienen hielo de agua, que podría proporcionar agua potable, oxígeno y combustible para cohetes.

deep.x: The Moon's axis is barely tilted (about 1.5°), so near the poles some crater floors never see sunlight. These "permanently shadowed regions" are among the coldest places in the Solar System, around −240 °C, cold enough to trap water ice for billions of years.

steps: Comets and solar wind bring water

deep.x: Evidence

x: India's Chandrayaan-1 (2008) mapped water ice signatures with a NASA instrument
NASA's LCROSS (2009) crashed into a crater and found water in the plume
Chandrayaan-3 landed near the south pole in 2023

deep.x: Why it's valuable
Light and power
Some ridges nearby are almost always sunlit, ideal for solar panels, right next to the dark ice-filled craters.
Making fuel on the Moon could turn it into a refuelling station for deeper missions.

cards.title: Gateway
cards.text: El Lunar Gateway es una pequeña estación prevista en órbita lunar, construida por la NASA, la ESA, Japón y Canadá, para apoyar los alunizajes.

deep.x: The Lunar Gateway is a planned small space station in a highly elliptical "near-rectilinear halo orbit" around the Moon. Much smaller than the ISS, it would host crews for short stays and serve as a staging point for landings.
Why that orbit?

The orbit swings close over the lunar south pole and far out over the north. It's stable, needs little fuel to maintain, keeps constant contact with Earth and is reachable from Earth and lunar landers.
European role
ESA contributes habitation and refuelling modules and the ESPRIT communications module. In return, European astronauts are to fly to the Moon.
Uncertain future
Gateway's schedule and scope have changed as budgets and priorities shift, and its future has been debated in US budget discussions.
Space programmes depend on politics as much as engineering; plans often change.

cards.title: Humanos a Marte
cards.text: Enviar personas a Marte exige cohetes enormes, protección contra la radiación, soporte vital durante años y una forma de volver. La mayoría de los planes apuntan a la década de 2030 o más tarde.

deep.x: A crewed Mars mission is far harder than Apollo. A round trip with today's propulsion takes roughly 2–3 years, including waiting on Mars for planets to realign.
The big challenges
Landing is the hardest part

Mars' thin air is too thin for parachutes to slow heavy craft enough, but too thick to ignore. Landing a crew vehicle of tens of tonnes will need supersonic retro-rockets, a technique still being developed.
Who's planning

x: NASA's long-term Moon-to-Mars plans
SpaceX's Starship, designed for Mars cargo and crew
China's stated goals for Mars sample return and later crews

deep.w: We could go to Mars next year if we wanted
deep.r: Radiation, landing and life support remain unsolved at crewed scale

deep.x: Mars is about 150 times farther than the Moon at its closest; help from Earth would take months.

cards.title: Turismo espacial
cards.text: Desde 2021, empresas privadas han llevado a turistas de pago al borde del espacio y a la órbita. Los billetes cuestan desde cientos de miles hasta decenas de millones de dólares.

deep.x: Space tourism now comes in two kinds. Suborbital flights go up about 80–100 km for a few minutes of weightlessness and a view of Earth's curvature. Orbital flights circle Earth for days and cost far more.
Milestones

events.l: Dennis Tito, first space tourist on the ISS
Virgin Galactic and Blue Origin crewed flights

deep.x: Where is space?
Two definitions are used: the Kármán line at 100 km, used internationally, and 80 km, used by the US Air Force and NASA for astronaut wings.
Debates

x: Carbon emissions and soot from rockets in the upper atmosphere
Safety and regulation of private flights
Whether it's a luxury for the rich or a path to cheaper access for everyone

deep.x: Space tourists still need medical checks and days to weeks of training, especially for orbital flights.

cards.title: Minería de asteroides

steps: Hallar un asteroide rico en metal

cards.text: Algunos asteroides contienen metales como níquel, hierro y platino. Extraerlos podría abastecer a una futura industria espacial, pero todavía no es rentable.

deep.x: Some asteroids are rich in metals like iron, nickel, cobalt and platinum-group metals; others contain water and carbon compounds. In space, the most valuable resource may be water, for fuel and life support, rather than gold.
Psyche

NASA's Psyche mission, launched in 2023, will arrive in 2029 at asteroid 16 Psyche, which may be the exposed metal core of a shattered protoplanet. Headlines valued its metal at quadrillions of dollars, but that number is meaningless: flooding the market would crash prices.
Why not yet?

x: Getting there and back is slow and costly
Extracting and processing in microgravity is unsolved
Bringing large amounts of metal to Earth isn't economic

deep.x: Legal questions
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty forbids national claims, but some countries, including the USA and Luxembourg, have passed laws letting companies own resources they extract. Others disagree.
Space mining will likely start with water for in-space use, long before metals are shipped to Earth.

cards.title: Viajes interestelares
cards.text: La estrella más cercana está a 4,2 años luz; la Voyager tardaría unos 75 000 años. Ideas como sondas diminutas impulsadas por láser podrían reducirlo a décadas.

deep.x: Proxima Centauri is 4.2 light-years away: 40 trillion km. Voyager 1, moving at 17 km/s, would take about 75,000 years to cover that distance. Reaching another star within a human lifetime needs radically new propulsion.
Breakthrough Starshot

Announced in 2016, this concept would launch thousands of gram-scale chips on ultra-thin light sails, pushed by a huge ground-based laser array to about 20% of light speed. They'd reach Alpha Centauri in about 20 years and send back images.

steps: Tiny chip on a light sail

deep.x: Huge challenges

x: A laser array of about 100 gigawatts
Sails surviving intense laser heating
Surviving impacts with interstellar dust at 60,000 km/s
Sending signals home from tiny transmitters

deep.x: Generation ships
Some imagine slow ships where generations live and die during a voyage of centuries. It raises deep questions about consent and survival.
A one-tonne probe at 20% of light speed would carry kinetic energy comparable to hundreds of nuclear weapons, which is why only tiny probes are proposed.

cards.title: Los próximos telescopios espaciales

steps: Tapar el brillo de la estrella

cards.text: Los telescopios de nueva generación quieren fotografiar exoplanetas parecidos a la Tierra y analizar su aire en busca de señales de vida, como oxígeno y metano juntos.

deep.x: The next generation of telescopes aims to answer: are there other Earths with signs of life? The challenge is enormous: an Earth-like planet is about 10 billion times fainter than its star in visible light.

items.b: ESA, Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars, ~2026

deep.x: Blocking the starlight

To see a faint planet next to a bright star, telescopes use a coronagraph inside or a "starshade" flying far in front, both designed to block the star's glare while letting the planet's light through.
Biosignatures
Splitting a planet's light reveals its air. Oxygen, ozone, methane and water together, out of chemical balance, would be a strong hint of life.
On the ground
The Extremely Large Telescope, with a 39 m mirror, may detect oxygen on nearby rocky planets around small stars from the ground.
The first images of an Earth-like planet will be just a few pixels, but those pixels could answer one of humanity's oldest questions.

cards.title: Derecho espacial

items: Cada país responde de sus naves

cards.text: El Tratado del Espacio Exterior de 1967 establece que ningún país puede reclamar la Luna ni los planetas, y que el espacio es libre para que todos lo exploren de forma pacífica. La minería de recursos sigue en debate.

deep.x: Space law began with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, now ratified by over 110 countries. It treats space as "the province of all mankind".

items: No national claims on celestial bodies
Peaceful use of the Moon and planets
States responsible for their private companies

deep.x: Other treaties
The Artemis Accords

Since 2020, dozens of countries have signed the Artemis Accords, non-binding principles for peaceful exploration: transparency, sharing data, avoiding interference and protecting historic sites like Apollo landing sites.
Open questions

x: Who can extract and own space resources?
How should debris and traffic be managed?
How to prevent conflict and weapons in space?

deep.x: The Apollo 11 landing site has no legal protection under international law yet; the Accords encourage preserving it.

cards.title: ¿Por qué explorar?

items: Datos del tiempo y el clima

cards.text: La investigación espacial nos ha dado la navegación por satélite, las previsiones del tiempo, mejores técnicas de imagen médica y filtros de agua, y responde a la pregunta más antigua: ¿estamos solos?

deep.x: Space programmes cost money that could be spent on Earth, so the question is fair. Supporters point to practical benefits, scientific knowledge, economic growth and inspiration.

items: Science: understanding the universe and Earth

deep.x: Spin-offs
Costs in perspective
NASA's budget is about 0.4% of US federal spending. ESA's budget is roughly the cost of a cinema ticket per European each year.
Earth benefits most
Climate monitoring, disaster response, food security and navigation all depend on satellites. Understanding Venus and Mars helps us understand climate on Earth.
As Apollo 8 astronaut Bill Anders put it, "We came all this way to explore the Moon, and the most important thing is that we discovered the Earth."

options: Hay hielo de agua en cráteres en sombra
quiz.explain: Agua para respirar, beber y hacer combustible.

quiz.explain: El espacio es de todos.
